the greatest experiment in practioal social- ism the world has ever seen. Not content with a municipal ownership of street railroads, electric and gas lighting plants, water supplies and telephones in several cities, the municipal corpora- tions build dwellings for workingmen, run hotels and erect and operate magnificent baths. In Liver- pool tee Council has gone SO far as to charge part of what should be the rent from municipal houses occupied by workingmen as homes against the taxes of the community. Recurring to the subject of electric street railway:a, Boyle says that the first line was E tarted in Liverpool a few days ag4, and he, describe, the equipment. For the benefit of American manufacturers of electrical plants, fit- tings, and rails, the Consul sets forth the best means for these to put themselves in position to secure valuable contracts, though he points out a strong prejudice on the part of a large class of people in the cities against the award of contracts to foreigners. Toe Liverpool line is an overhead trolley, a committee of experts claiming to have discovered that the underground conduit system installed in New York, Washington and Baltimore is a failure. He speaks of several other systems of electric car propulsion which have b en brought forward in England as novelties, but which are well known here, such as the surface contact syetem.A scheme under way, he says, is to connect Liverpool with all the manufacturing towns within a radius of seventeen miles by light suburban elec- tric street railroads, which will carry passengers in the day time and freight at night." If Mr. Roberts wants.to know more of the doings of socialism he may turn his enquiries to Glasgow where. unless I am mistaken, he may learn bow the geol citizens of that canny town propose to start the new year clear of the tax gatherer. These are steps in the right direction and if Warrington can matinee its gas and water works, I don't see why it should no:. be able to manage successfully its own system of trams, and so help on socialie.m. The ex- istence of Mr. Pecksniff has ever been a puzzle to me. Feeling snug and smug in his own righteous way, he is always thanking God he is not as other men are. He seems to forget entirely that the one fundamental doctrine in Christ's teachings was the equality of men before God, and consequently the equality of men on God's earth. I have beside me an article on the Equality of man " written by "Verax," y ars ago, and I know and accept the qualifications of the statement, and yet when I read the following in an English paper, not yet a month old, I asked myself the question, can the Christian opponents of socialism be sati=fied with such a state of things? The aWcle in quest:on tells a pitiful tale of the miseries of the London sempstrese, which, in spite of the retort of the House of Loris Committee on the sweating system, is little better to-day than it was 50 are ago,when Tom Hord wrote his memor- able " Song of the Shirt." Authentic figures quoted show that for making the average blouse a good semrsiress receives about three halfpence, and out of that she has to provide her own cotton I A sample case is given of two expert" hands" who were employed for a little over a week, 12 hours a day, in making dozen velvet and silk blouses, at one and sixpence a dozen, and their nett earnings, after paying ler cetton, and expenses fcr fetching and carrying back the work, amoeived to 2e. 100. each. Two and tenpence halfpenny for a week's labour! The cheap blouse is no the only one taken into consideretion ; for the eil!r blouse the pay is a little Well--; and on a blouse sced for 18i or 24g. the maker receives the princely sum of Bkl. This is -imply shocking. Eightpence half- penny out of t wenty-five shillings ! The material, we may say, costs from eight to twelve shillings at the outside. Where does the rest go to? Other figures are given, all pointing to an equally sqaalid poverty and ill-paid toil. This is simply terrible, and should urge ram and women on to do anything and everything to put a stop to such a state of things.

And yet what can be done? I believe in the pearreful and evolutionary growth of things. In writing this letter I started out with the intention of keeping to things pilitical, and those American, but my feelings have somewhat run away with me. In the association of ideas growing out of American expansion,and the pos3ibility of John and Jonathan becoming better frien,ls. I have wandered off into an oft trodden path. and so must leave the subject for future treatment. Wishing all ray readers a happy new year, I 84 them to notice my new ad- dress, 1318, Ouerrer-street, 8 F.

div.head: BOVRIL V.
div.p: BOVRIL V.
INFLUENZA.

As a preventive of Influenza, Bovril is supreme, because it gives that healthy tone and warmth to the body which alone offers effectual resistance to the attacks of the dreaded disease from which so many suffer in winter time.

Hasty meals, most often taken at irregular hours, engender that chilly discomfort and de- pression of spirits when the body is least imper- vious to the germs of influenza. A cup of Bovril is all that is required as a mainstay and a warmth-giver. Taken between breakfast and lunch, it is an admirable stimulant..

Bovril is not only a preventive of Influenza, but renders invaluable assistance in ridding the system of an attack. When the symptoms develop—headaches, chilly sensations,nervous- n.ess, and loss of appetite—Bovril will be found most acceptable as an appetising, stimulating, and easily assimilable food, strengthening the system when strength is most needed; when the attack has subsided, prod:aptly renew- ing the vital forces, and bringing about a com- plete recovery.

div.head: JUST A TALK.
div.p: JUST A TALK.
(BY ,JR. H. W lIITIIAM )

Another year has rolled by, and what an eventful enne. Looking over the events of the past. twelve months I cannot help thinking that they,as a whole, mark a point of departure, or, shall I say, a point from', which we start out to enterprises of which we have not before dreamed. The one that seems likely to take most shape, and to be fraught with more interest to the world at large is an outcome of the short but decisive war between Jonathanomd the Don. Who among us could foresee, twelve months ago, that an Areerican journal would put- lish these lines? " With John ant Jonathan sworn to atm I Shoulder to shoolder. hand by hand. Pieties and peace shall build their throne From tropic se. to frozen zone " To realise ell that underlies the words of the poet is to grasp the idea that the time may not be far distant, when the sword may with confidence be beaten into the ploughshare, and a certain halt be called in the wild and ruinous system now obtain- ing among the so-called civilised nations of the earth in the taXstion necessary for the maintenance of such immense standing armies and ;navies. The numbers of soldiers being maintained, and the amount of money drawn from labour (I suppose no one will deny that the armies and navies .are maintained by laboar,) finds its way into the daily press, but it seems to have little effect on the masses. As a matter of fact the figures in each case are so outrageeusly immense that one fails to grasp their significance and so idly paoses them on. And yet, are we justified in so doing? I think not. We may fret and weep at the thought that so much of our toil is being devoted to the civilizing pur- poses of war and bloodshed. We ma) lament that the best brains in the Parliaments of the world are devoted to the controlling and building of these armies and naviee, and we may gnash our teeth at the thought that the best science of the day is either devoted to the task of building an impregnable war ship or else constructing guns that nothing can resist. It is all in vain. As the years roll on our scientific men seem to become more daring; the more they achieve, and the more they see there is to achieve. There seems to be a necessity in this. Governments wishful to Emil en- tangling alliances, seem to be forced whether t hey will or no, to form alliances, and "territorial ex- pansion "becomes a household word in the great- *et republic the world has even seen. To me, it seems that the science, and the expansion above re- ferred to can have but one ultimate goal,and shortly we may see.—t hat, "The world's great peacsewill have begun." It, is said that "genius is reeolution- izing industry with its labour saving inventiors, and science ia draoging from their hiding places the secrets of nature,' to what purpose, one may ask, .if not foe the alleviation of the woes of man We may be sure that the signs of the times, to which I have referred, point to the great truth that the struggle in the future for existence will be less with the sword than with the weapons of indu4ry and commerce. Then will come the time, when science turned into its best and loftiest channel, will find work ready to its hand, in making it possible for a half-employed world to produce without all the sorrow and tears we now have, all that is needed fonts consumption. This is rank socialiem some of my readers may say, and we have the word of Mr Councillor Relieve • for it, that," S.ociallsm is coercion, so we will have , none of it." When I read in the " Examieer," the remarks of Councillor Roberts, my thoughts flew • back to other data. I remembered the time when be, as well as myself, would have used all the .coercion possible to have forced the Home Rule Bill through the House ef Lerds. Ile believed it was Iright, and for the good of the people, so did I, none the less, be would have used coercion. He call have no kick now, if socialists force upon him what they believe to be for the good of all. Like all the great epoch making movements of the past, Socialism is making its way by paths little noticed, and yet surely. For instance I take up the "San Francisco Chronicle "and read the following which may be news to Mr. Roberts: " W aelaing- ton, December 15.—United States Consul Boyle at Liverpool has communicated to the State Depart- enent some interesting information respecting the great change that has taken place in England in the matter of street rtiilwaye. Ile save that from being one of the most backward in the matter of providing such accommodatione,the Citiee of Great Britian are now moving on an enormous scale tr- ward their construct on. Boyle describes this move- ment as one feature of the rernerkable municipal socialism which is taking poseessiou of British cit'ee -verifying the comment of Lord Ropebery that the London -County Council was conducting

div.head: CONTINENTAL ENTHUSIASM.
div.p: CONTINENTAL ENTHUSIASM.
EY W. T. STEAD.

We have the literary men with us. An undue suspicion of the interference of bookmen in national questions exists in some quarters, but that objection cannot apply to Dr. Conan Doyle and Mr. Bernard Shaw, who were the principal speakers at the Hindhead meeting. These are men of the world as well as writers of books. Dr. Doyle is a tuJdern apostle of muscularity. He has ventured to glorify the ancient prize ring. Yet he is an enthusiast for international peace. He believes in the lofty and unselfish aims which inspire the Czar, and lie has not hesitated to proclaim his ()Onion.

Sunday's meeting at Leeds was, in many respects, a very remarkable gathering. The Coliseum was crowded to the doors nearly a quarter of an hour Pt fore the meeting began. Proceedings were from Crst to last unanimous and enthusiastic. Sir James Kitson, who was in the chair, made a note- worthy speech. He is one of the few members of l'arlinment who have recently travelled in Russia. Pis testimony as to the anxiety not only of the Czar, but of his most powerful Ministers, to divert the expenditure on armaments to the construction of railways was received with intense interest by the crowded audience. Sir James Kitson is iimeensely impressed with the great field for indielrial development which is to be found in the Riesian Empire, and being a wise and prudent with a good eye to the main chance, he has brcn one of the first to profit by the opening up of this field for Eritish enterprise. Mr. Herbert Gladeone, who wrote a letter strongly supporting the Crusade, and declaring that its importance was greater than. that of any other movement at present before the country, has also travelled in Russia, as far as the Caspian. He and Sir James Kitson drove with perfect security through mountain passes which, a few years before, had been, infested with brigands, but which are now as safe as the road Letween Leeds and Harro- Ore No inure gratirring testimonies to the evilising influence of Ressia in Asia could have hern desired than these which lay before the people of Leeds.

A very mistaken idea appears to pievail in some cuarters—that the meetings which are being held all over the country are being got up by the Crusaders in London. As a matter of fact., the irovement is breaking cut on all sides in a way wh•ch renders it impossible for the headquarters to deal with the matter. Take, for instance, the town's meetings at Liverpool and Hull. Both of those were got up entirely by the townspeople. They were summoned by the Chief Magistrate, and addressed by local speakers. No representative was present at either one or the other from out- side, but in Loth of these great sea-ports—one on. the east and the other in the west coast of England— 7rqceedings were unanimous, the speeches hearty and the riteetings crowded. .

There is no doubt- an immense advantage in having evidence of the popular feeling, but it is much to be desired that those who are holding public meetings should, in all cases, communicate with headquarters, if only for the purpose of securing the adoption of a uniform resolution in favour of the election of delegates to the National Convention, which will probably be held in March. In places where the resolution in support of the Conference has been passed, without an accom- panying resolution appointing delegates in the pro- portion of one to every 10,000 of the population, it vill probably be found better for the speakers and the secretary to be considered as an informal committee of selection, and for them to nominate representatives of their towns to the Convention ; but it would be much better if the resolution could be formally put to the meeting nominating a com- mit Ise of selection.

The enrolment or volunteers nas gone on at every meeting which I have addressed. Here, also, the need of local organisation is vital. The procedure is simple. At. the close of each meeting those who are willing to volunteer for three months' service for peace are requested to come forward, pay their shillings, receive their badges, and enrol themselves as volunteers. As each volunteer under- takes to obtain two other volunteers, he should wceive two forms of enrolment for his recruits, two badges on credit, and three forms of the Memorial—one for himself and one for each of his two recruits. By this means it will be possible, after even a small nucleus of volunteers, to multiply and increase their number so ..s to work the whole district. At Lambeth, on Sunday last,' where the volunteers were first enrolled, 122 were obtained, at St. Austell between 60 and 70, at Plymouth over 100, at Rochdale 70, at Streatham about 30; while at Leeds it is expected they will exceed those at any ether place. The organisation for enrolling volunteers has been usually improvised at an after meeting. At Rochdale, the Mayor, who presided over the town's meeting with his chain of office, accepted the post of Treasurer, and received the shillings on the spot. It is also necessary to have one or more places in the town where the badges can he issued and volunteers enlisted. Tradesmen in leading thoroughfares usually volunteer to allow their shops to be used as recruiting offices. The reporting of the meetings of the Crusaders varies amusingly. The largest and best reports, by far, have been those which appeared in the Plymouth papers. They devoted from five to seven columns of their space to the report of the town's meeting. The Manchester Guardian and the St. Peiersburg Gazette are the only daily papers which, so far, have told off a special correspondent to follow the Crusaders. _ _ _

Although one finds little evidence of the fact in the great dailies, London is giving a support to this movement which it extends to few agitations. For every meeting that is held, two are immediately requested. Each post brings requests for help and information, which will be of value in the organ sa- ton of gatherings. The agenda which was placed hefcre the General Committee at its meeting on Monday had only been prepared on the Friday. It contained a list of the meetings arranged. Between the time of sending the copy to the printers and its actual discussion no less than five more meetings had beer. arranged in the capital alone, and half a score others were in active preparation. These are facts that cannot be avoided, and that can only be igrored for a time. Hackney, Streatham, Westminster, and Walworth all speak unmistakably of an aroused public sentiment. From the first, Earl Grey, vho pres•des - at the meeting in the N,..wcastle Town Hall, has thrown himself into the Peace Crusade with characteristic energy and enthusiasm. He has not only consented to take the chair at a meeting,' he is primarily responsible for the ho!ding and the oreanisation of one of the most notable demonstrations since the commencement of the Crusade. The adherence of no other man could have done so much for the cause of peace in the North of England. Earl Grey is a man about whom all parties rally. Even those who now differ from him politically respect and admire him personally. The way in which he has thrown his influence into the scale for peace has roused the whole North of England. Nor has he contented himself with active work. The largest cheque to the funds of the Crusade, received last week, was one for £5O, bearing the signature "Grey."

On the Continent the interest in the pilgrimage of peace grows daily. One of the odd things illustrating this was the imperious demand from Paris that a day should be fixed for the arrival of the delegates, because Madame Sarah Bernhardt and other distinguished theatrical artistes who had promised to assist at a soirée to be given in their honour at the office of the Fronde must know a good whi, ahead, in order to keep the evening clear.

What with soirees with Sarah Bernhardt, and "Te Deums " in the Cathedrals, and receptions by the Burgomasters, the pilgrims of peace are likely to have an interesting and exciting time. It has been dvided that each of the smaller States shall send two delegates. If, as is at present talked of, Nansen and Biiirnsen are chosen as the delegates from Norway, the International Crusaders will not be lacking in elements of universal interest.

" were the words which were addressed to him by a stout, sleek, well-groomed person with an unctuous voice, whom he did not remember to have seen before. _

"I beg your pardon, sir; you haw; the advantage of me," was his lordship's rather stttT rejoinder. But mere hauteur, unaccompanied by positive rudeness, was ineffectual as a snub to the gerltlii- man in question, who infused a comical air of astonishment into both his manner and his speer;h, as he retorted: • _ _
"What! You don't remember me? Why, We were introdooced one night at the 'ouse of the Princess Delilah of Courland. Now, ..then, do;fin recollect who I am?" _
"In afraid I must plead guilty to forg ness."

"Well, only fancy that now! I am Mr. Mosenthal, the great city stockbroker. You must know me very well by name, and I can givP y,,tt rather good tip, if you like. Shall I come round to your place-" "Excuse me, some ladies over there are anxious to see me at once, and I do not like to keep ladies waiting," said Lord Alfred hurriedly, and then, very much to his own annoyance, Mr. Sammie Mosenthal was deprived of the pleasure of being seen in familiar confabulation with a •"real live lord." _ .

How very late you are to-night," said the latter, a few moments afterwards to Miss Rizzen- Quicke. "I began to be afraid you were not coming." "Father had a caller," said Folly regretfully. "He came on business at a most awkward time, and couldn't be got rid of in a hurry. In fact, both mother and I were ready to start before the man went away, and then we had to wait until father had put evening dress on. I was fidgeting all the time we were waiting, for I knew we should miss more than half the opera, and what is the use of seeing only the tail end of a piece? " "Why, do you really come to the theatre to see the opera itself ? " "Of course I do. What else should I come for ? "
_ "The same reason that brings all the rest of us. We come to look at each other, and admire each other, and the opera itself is merely a means to that end."
"I•say," interjected Mr. Rizzen-Quicke, "I'm blest if that Princess Delilah hasn't got your stone on, Jane."

• "No, not the same," corrected Lord Alfred, "but one very much like it." "Anyways, John Mills didn't think there was another like it, and there isn't a diamond among all the hundreds that are worn in this theatre to- night that blazes like that star-sapphire. But, of course, that couldn't be the same stone. John said there was only another one in the world that partly came up to it, so that must be the other one, and I wish he was here to-night to look at it. Poor John! I wonder what has really become of him ? "

"Father," whispered Polly, "you know what a job we had to persuade mother to come out and enjoy herself to-night? She is getting so anxious about Teddy that she would mope all day if we would let her, and if you begin talking about John Mills you will make her as melancholy as ever again." Thus being reminded that he had set himself the task of trying to reconcile his wife to Teddy's delayed return, Mr. Rizzen-Quicke forced himself to put on an air of comparative jollity. But Lord Alfred became imbued with an ad conviction that the absences of John Mills and Teddy Quicke were mysteriously connected with each other. And, meanwhile, the progress of events was tending to shew what an awful truth underlay:this conviction.
CHAPTER X. A LUCKY ACCIDENT.

When Mr., Mrs., and Miss Rizzen-Quicke reached home from Covent Garden Theatre, they were surprised to find an unusual air of activity pervading the establishment. Lights were blazing in every room, nearly all the servants were in tribulative evidence, and a couple of policemen helped to demonstrate the fact that some event of exceptional importance had occurred during their absence., "Who#' he - 9 " Rizzen-I

...iat's the matter r - inquires _r. Quicke, addressing the staid butler, who appeared to be in that euriuos state of mini which is half afraid to tell an unpleasant truth, yet wholly reluctant to miss the unwonted sensation of watching the effect upon others of the unpleasant truth which has to be told. "It was most unforeseen, sir," he said nervously, _ _

"and I hope you won't hold us responsible for ft. One or two of us had gone to bed, and the rest were spending the evening quietly, our duties for the day being over, when all at once we heard a terrific crash upstairs. As soon as we could make out which room the noise seemed to come from, some of us ran to madam's room, and found the window open. Everything in the room was in con- fusion, and it was easy to see that some strangers had been in it." - -

"Good Heavens, man I " interrupted Mr. ' Quicke, "what on earth are you driving at? Why don't you tell me at once what has happened' Have there been burglars in the house ? " "Yes, sir, that's what's the matter. They have ransacked madam's room, and gone out through the window on to the portico, smashing one of the windows as they went. "And have they got clear away ? " "l'm afraid they have, sir." "What have they taken with them ? " "The lady's maid says that the mistress's jewel case has gone, and I don't know what besides." By this time Mrs. Quicke was finding out for herself what had been taken out of her room, for directly she gathered that it had been "burgled," she made all haste to go thither, being preceded by the fleeter-footed Polly. It did not take long: to realise the full extent of the depredations, for in spite of the butler's assertion that the whole !om was in confusion, very little was disturbed beyond such drawers and receptacles as were most likely to con- tain jewel-cases, and it was upon these receptacles that the lathes naturally bestowed their first atten- tion. They could not examine the two jewel-cases which had been stored therein, for they had beeq stolen, together with some valuable diamonds and emeralds, as well as the priceless star-sapphire which Mrs. Rizzen-Quicke had felt reluctant to year or to inspect until the mystery of John Mills's disappearance had been cleared up. indeed, she had carried this feeling so far that she had never even looked at the jewel since the day On which it had first become known that John was no longer to be found in his usual haunts. As a matter of course the police were put into possession of all the Information which could be presumed to assist them in bringing the burglary home to its perpetrators, and on the day subse- quent to the event, Mr. Quicke was closeted for a long time with various detectives, who made their examinations, picked up several supposed clues, eventually followed these clues up, and found that they led to nowhere. "Upon my word," mused the Gold King, "the happiest people must be the ones who have just enough to keep them comfortably, but not enough to lose. Here am I, worried to death because my wife has had her jewel-case stolen from her, and ho,arise my son has taken French leave without 'hewing the slightest consideration for our feelings. 11 I had been a poorer man Teddy would have had to work instead of flying round after princesses and yachts, and Jane wouldn't have had any jewels worth stealing. But there, we shall forget it all when Teddy comes back, and if I can't buy another star-sapphire for my wife, I can buy her a shop- windowful of jewels if she wants them. So I'll put the whole business out of my head, and we thre3 will have drive in the park. What did you N.;.y, Clayton ? " Clayton was the bearer of a card on a silver ealver, ,and on looking at this card Mr. Rizzen- luicke saw inscribed on it the words: "Edgar - -.c.iiman, private detective." .• Oh, bother!" he exclaimed. "Surely plenty of detectives have got their fingers into the pie by this time, and I won't employ any more of them. Clayton, tell the man I'm engaged. Yet, stay, I've heard that private detectives have sometimes solved mysteries which the men from Scotland Yard couldn't manage, and perhaps this man is one of the clever ones. Anyhow, the detectives employed so far haven't shewn themselves very useful, so I've half a mind to give this fellow a turn. He might be able to find, something out about John Mills as well as about the star- sapphire." , Having formed this opinion, Mr. Rizzen-Quicke acted upon it at once, with the result that the new detective was ushered into his presence forthwith. He proved to be very tall, very stout, and very grizzled, giving the impression that he was well on towards his sixtieth year. But he Am I still brisk and active, and the piercing bia(;1: eyp, from beneath his bushy eyebrov

PRINCESS DELILAH.

By MRS. GEORGE CORBETT, Author of "When the Sea Gives up its Dead," "The Prince Physician," "The Vindication of Olive Trevethick," "The Star of Yukon," "The Adventures of an Ugly Girl," "Deb o' Molly's," "A Fair Blockade Runner," Ito.

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS: John Mills, part owner of a gold mine and of a most valuable star-sapphire, loses all to the millionaire, Mr. Rizzen-Quicke, at gambling. Rizzen-Quicke gives it him back on the condition that he never gambles again. In gratitude Mills gives the star-sapphire to his benefactor's wife. Meanwhile two aristocratio scoundrels, Prince Carlos of Mitylene and the Duke of Solltesein, are plotting with a stockbroker named Mosenthal to float a bogus gold-makers' company, and incidentally they hope to capture some of the wealth of Rizzen-Quicke and Mills. John Mills mysteriously disappears after withdrawing 4,000 sovereigns from his bank. Teddy Rizzen-Quicke falls in love with the Princess Delilah, who has some mysterious connection with the Prince and the Duke. She promises to marry Teddy if he can secure the star-sapphire for her. It is Mrs. Rizzen- Quicke's ambition that her son should marry the Princess, and her daughter, Polly, Prince Carlos. Teddy disappears in a mysterious way after cashing a large cheque wholly in sovereigns. The star- sapphire also goes. Lord Alfred Vavasour-Pomeroy, who has fallen in love with Polly Rizzen-Quicke, thinks there is something sinister in the disappear- ances of Mills and of Teddy, and he determines to make inquiries carefully and privately.
CHAPTER IX.
WERE THERE TWO STAR-SAPPHIRES?

The Opera season was proving an unusually successful one, a circuinstance which is satisfactory both for_ the xho provide the entertainment and for those wFo' go to witness it. Given a crowded house there is a certainty of seeing many well- known faces, and of having much gorgeous raiment to criticise, and when such social stars as the Princess Delilah are among the audience,- they are apt to eclipse the vocal stars who grace the foot- lights. So, at least, thought a great many people to whom the beauty of the latter was a revelation. All knew her by name, and some had heard such reports of her matchless loveliness and her unlimited wealth, that they were prepared to see something quite out of the common. Yet nothing they had imagined came up to the actual reality. Lady Flora Vavasour-Pomeroy,-who was with her people in their' box, turned to her brother and remarked regretfully: "Alfy, you don't know how vicious I feel! The Princess Delilah is looking ihdre 'innocently heavenly than ever, and what man in his senses will trouble to look at. an insignificant little being like me, when he can feast his"eyes"upon:her ? I suppose there is nothing extraordinary in that white satin gown she is wearing, but I don't believe it would suit anyone else half so well." "Possibly not," assented Lord Alfred. "Her pale golden hair, delicate complexion, and melting- blue eyes, are thoroughly in harmony with her attire, and if her mind matches her beauty, she is a subject for the angels to rejoice over. But, what- ever the angels may think of her, she isn't altogether to my taste. I like something a little more natural and human."
"Like Miss Biz;el-Quicke, for instance?" "Yes, like P /."

"Oh, it's come to Polly, has it ? That sounds hopeful. Well, I'm not surprised, dear boy. She's a jolly girl, and she possesses the additional attraction to me of not being the sort of individual whom I shall be everlastingly asked to look up to and adulate at a respectful distance. But when am I to call upon her in a sisterly manner? And why isn't she here to-night? " One question at a time, my dear girl. In answer to the first one, I shall be very much happier than I am at present when I can assure you that there is a certainty of her becoming your sister. The answer to the second one is easier to give. The Rizzen-Quickes intended to be here to-night, and I have no doubt they will turn up yet. I expect something has happened to detain them." "And, meanwhile, you have to console yourself with talking to me and looking at the iirincess Delilah. Why, Alfy, did you ever see such a beautiful gem as that which forms the pendant to her necklace? It is perfectly marvellous! Lord Alfred had already been struck by the more than usual radiance of the Princess's jewels, and he was already comparing the gem which occupied the post of honour with the star-sapphire which had played so conspicuous a part at the reception given by Mr. and Mrs. Rizzen-Quicke. "Of course thq thing is impossible," he told himself. "But I ?A:mid almost swear that they are one and the sane atone." "I say, P10t?.," he; saialo his sister, "do you mind excusing me for five minutes, while Igo to the Princess Delilah's box? I have a fancy for inspecting that jewel more closley, for it is astonishingly like Mrs. Rizzen-Quicke's star- sapphire, and I was under the impression that there was but one other in the world that could even nearly approach it." One of Lady Flora's most persistent admirers put in an appearance at this moment, and she was, therefore, the more readily inclined to condone the absence of her brother, who exchanged greetings with two or three friends before he passed on to the box which enshrined the most beautiful woman in the house.

She welcomed him with a great shesv of cordiality; invited him to sit by her side for a little, and made a few comments upon various personages in the audience who attracted her atten- tion. Then, as she caught him looking in a puzzled manner at her necklace-pendant, she smilingly challenged his admiration for it. "I see you are looking at my beautiful star- sapphire," she observed, with an exceedingly well- pleased air. "I do not want people to imagine that I am like a vain little child, or that I am asking you to admire, me, but I certainly do want you to notice my star-sapphire. Ever since I saw the one which that curious John Mills gave to Mrs. Rizzen-Quicke, I have been dying to possess one like it. It was mentioned at the time that there was only one other in the world that bore any resemblance to it, and I forthwith resolved to become the possessor of that other. With unlimited resources at one's command, one can even buy a kingdom, and as I have no need to be afraid of spending money, I have been able to realise my ambition.—And that is the history of my star-sapphire." "Do you know," said Lord Alfred meditatively, "the beauty of that jewel strikes me as positively unearthly, and those restless stars of light remind me of the Evil Eye." "Nonsense! I had no idea you were super- stitious, and I have a strong objection to having any of my property invested with ominous qualities." "I beg your pardon, Princess. I was merely alluding to the strange loveliness of the jewel, and even if its past history had been associated with anything uncanny or evil, it would naturally enter upon a new era as soon as it came under your influence."

"You would make a charming courtier, Lord Alfred, and if ever I come into the Kingdom which certain soothsayers have foretold is in store for me, I shall know where to look for a flatterer who can put an air of truth on all he says. But, look! there come the Gold King and his wife and daughter at last. I wonder if Mrs. Rizzen-Quicke is wearing her star-sapphire? I shall never rest satisfied until I have been able to compare hers with mine."

"Shall I go and make inquiries for you ? " "Well, no, that would look rather absurd, wouldn't it? But there will be no harm in telling Mrs. Rizzen-Quicke that Mr. Stree has at last succeeded in procuring for me the only star- sapphire which is known to be in existence, besides her own."

Being thus practically dismissed, and having satisfied his curiosity concerning Princess Delilah's star-sapphire, Lord Alfred quietly made his way round to the Rizzen-Quicke's box, with a more thoughtful expression than usual on his face. "I was not mistaken," he mused; "there are a great many flaws in Princess Delilah's beauty. These, physically interpreted, would hardly be considered sufficiently important to be noticed, but they are indications of character which warn the intelligent observer to be on his guard against her. If I am to believe her eyebrows. which almost meet each other obliquely, near the roof of her nose, she is as accomplished a liar as it is possible to meet. Her nostrils, too, are just flat enough and wide spreading enough to shew that she is a schemer who might, perhaps, prove dangerous. Now I come to think of it, it is more than odd that nobody seems to know anything of the Princess Delilah's antecedents. If it were worth one's while, there might be some pleasurable excite- moat in trying to discover how much truth there is
possession or mum mental alertness without which nobody in the detective profession can hope to succeed.
"You must forgive me for intruding upon yol,' Mr. Rizzen-Quicke," . •truth I heard from Deteetii Yard friand of tuin, that there was e:c
a

shewing what I could do in a coy/ which you are interested: and I arn far my skill will ptove supericr to•I thought Mr. Quicke, "I enough anyhow. If lie. only fancies himself, he'll do." - "Well, sir," he answered, "I dar all about the -eobbtry before 3 doubt your friends told 14 ljt.ivtkoffered for the c! 'belonging-to iny wife." "Yes," said the strange.. -11 was in singt3h exterior. I kr.

"Except the thieves," corrected Mr. Rizzen- Quicke.' "Except the thieves, of course. But I must a:3 you to change your position if you will, sir. I cannot see your face as plainly as I would like." "Well, I'll be hanged!" thought Mr. Rizzen- Quicke, resenting the autocratic familiarity of his visitor as an uncalled for impertinence. "Where's his impudence to order me about ? " Yet, somehow, his anger evaporated, and he fell himself constrained to do exactly as he had been told.

_ "That will do," said the detective. "Now, then, Mr. Rizzen-Quicke, look into my face, and pay cloie attention to my words." • There was some more inward rebellion on the Gold King's part, followed by a speedy subjugation by a stronger will than his own; and then the visitor made a arange use of the evident ascendency he had over him.

"You have some writing materials, sir," he said, aftAr steadfastly fixing his eyes upon his vis-5,-vie fOr several minutes, during which time the latter seemed to gradually lose all power to control his own actions. "Sit down, and write to your wife a letter which I will dictate to you." Unresistingly, and in obedience to what was undoubtedly a strange hypnotic influence, Joseph Rizzen-Quicke sat down at his writing-table, drew a sheet of paper towards him, dipped his pen in the ink, and then wrote, to dictation: "Dear wife.' Then the visitor became conscious of a possible error.

"Wait a moment," he said. "How do yci..; usually address your wife when writing to her?" "Dear Jane," was the reply, given in a muffled voice that was curiously unlike Joseph Itizzen- Quicke' s. "Then give me that sheet of paper, and begin another one.". This order being also complied with, the letter began in earnest. "Dear Jane,—John Mills has written to tell me that he is ill and in trouble. He wants me to go to him at once, and it is just possible that I may not \get back until to-morrow morning. Don't worry about me, even if I can't manage to be back before to-morrow afternoon.—Your affectionate husband, Joe QUICKE." "Now then, fold that letter up, put it in an envelope,*ress it to your wife, and give it to me!' Colophon) as a baby, Mr. Dizzen-Quicke did as he was told. .
...mi., •w a...a vs/..“...• "Get your cheque-book at once," was the next command, "and sign a cheque for one thousand
pounds." Upon this order being complied with, the stranger intimated that he was ready to take his departure, and that Mr. Riz,zen-Quicke must follow him in five minutes. _ _

"When you reach the street," continued the extraordinary visitor, "you will get into a hansom which will be ready for you. Then you will drive to the Oxford-street Branch of the London and Westminster Bank, and change that cheque yourself for sovereigns. This money you will pack into a bag which you will find on the seat of the hansom, and you will replace this bag, containing the sovereigns, where you found it. You will also enter the hansom yourself, and the driver knows where to take you after that." Like a man who is in a hideous dream, Mr. Rizzen-Quicke knew that his state of subjugation to the will of another man was an utterly abnormal one. Yet he was capable of no further reflection than that, and even the ability to suspect possible danger to himself was quite annihilated for the time being. The butler soon afterwards saw him leave the house, and subsequently remarked to the house- keeper that the master had rather a strange look to-day. "He seems to me to be half asleep," he continued. "But I expect he's worrying about the burglary, and worry doesn't agree with him." Still obedient to the influence which was con- trolling his actions, Mr. Quicke did exactly as he was told—up to a certain point. He stepped into the hansom, which drew up to the kerb just as he reached it; noticed a well-made cowhide bag which stood on the seat; sat down beside it; was driven to the bank; entered the building with the cowhide bag in his hands; and presented hz. cheque, remarking that he wished to receive sovereigns in exchange. The cashier looked up in undisguised astonish- ment when he heard this unusual request. But he knew Mr. Quicke very well by sight, and did not make any intrusive remark to him, though he did manage to draw the attention of the cashier, who occupied the next desk to him, to the odd tralsaetion. _ _ _

"What a curious thing." he remarked, "for Mr. Ri- zen Quicke, a man who fairly rolls in money, and whose cheques would be honoured all the world over, to want to burthen himself with a thousand sovereigns." "Is that so? " was the observation. "It would be a funny thing for anybody else to do. But I am not so surprised at Mr. Rizzen-Quicke doing it as I should have been if his son had not done the same thin., a fortnight ago. Perhaps they want the gold to melt down into a table ornament or some- thing of the sort." Mr. Rizzen-Quicke lifted his bag on to the enunter, and the sovereigns were shovelled into it. Then, in the same dreamy, deliberate manner with which he had so far obeyed all the commands which had been imposed upon him by the man who had obtained such a malignant control over his mind, he emerged from the sank; took his seat in the hansom again without giving any directions to the .driver, and was driven off towards what had been intended to be his final destination.

But in his case Providence interposed to prevae the complete success of the hypnotist's experiment, and Providence showed itself this time in the guiles of a slippery pavement, which caused the horse's legs to slide from under it, and wrought havoc witl, the hansom, besides bringing the front of the vehicle and the fare's head into such violent contact with each other that a slight concussion of the brain was the outcome of the adventure. 'lhere was an immediate concourse of eager spectators, and most of them were so occupied with the unconscious gentleman that none of them had much attention to spare for the driver, who might reasonably have been supposed to do his beet to rescue his plunging horse from its uncomfortable position. But, for a cabman, he , was oddly indifferent to either his horse or his Vehicle. He had received a violent jerk, hut had managed to avoid being flung out of hi 4 seat. and he slid to the ground only an instant afr.cr Mr. Rizzen-Quicke had been injured. it was but the work of a second to possess him- self of the cowhide bag and its contents, and by the time people began to wonder . whether the cabman had been hurt or not, that worthy had put streets between himself and his inquirers. The accident occurred within five minute's drive of the Marble Arch, and a policeman, who was quickly on the spot, put his hand in Mr. Rizzen- Quicke's coat-pocket to see whether he ought to be sent to a hospital, or whether he lived near moue. to be sent home at once. _ .
His name and address was found inscrinea os• his card-case, and two perfectly reliable bystander: undertook to drive to his home with him in a four- wheeler.

It was seen by this time that the cabman had run off, and it was noted as a curious circumstance that there was about the hansom neither a number nor anything else which could give the least idea ,who owned it. It may be added that neither it nor the horse were ever claimed, though certain personages who figure in this history were afterwards able to make some not very inaccurate guesses concerning their ownership. There was much consternation when Mr. Rizzen- Quicke was brought home in an unconscious condi- tion by strangers, and it chanced that Lord Alfred Vavasour-Pomeroy was just entering the house as the cab drove un to the door. He was a young man of not more than eight-and-twenty, but he was ready-witeed and resourceful, and he proved him- self of invaluable service to the 'alarmed wife and daughter, though at present neither he uor they

div.p: enispectect that anything more abnormal than an - ordinary cab accident had occurred. Several doctors were speedily on the scene, and, to th^ --tlief of everybody, it was soon shewn that the she, Ito the brain was so slight as to give every •)mise of leaving no ill-effects behind it. Bui it Is the following day before the patient was able 3nverse intelligently, and meanwhile Mrs. •'...tuicke had received the letter which had eaten by her husband at the stranger's c,u. This caused much conjecture as to what have been Mr. Rizzen-Quicke's destination ht. was so unfortunately prevented from rig it. But it was not until after it was era safe to tax his brain with questions that isplcion of serious mischief began to enter e mind. lo you feel now, dear ? " she asked. "I
Rizz beel

am sr takinl to see you' looking all right again." "And vhy shouldn't I look all right?" he nel;ed . puzzled way, which shewed that he had btightest recollection of what had happened to him after a certain hour on the previous after- noon.

"Yon were slightly hurt in the cab accident." "What cab accident? I don't remember any- thing about a cab accident." "That is because your head was hurt a little. But it will come back to you by-and-bye. But tell me —How did you find John Mills? Or were you only going to him when the horse fell ? " "I really can't make head or tail of what you are talking about, Jane. I havn't heard a word about John, and I havn't the slightest idea where to find him: I only wish I had! " "But you wrote me a letter, to say that he had written to ask you to go and see him, as he was ill and in trouble. You also said that you were start- ing at once, and that you mightn't be back until to-morrow afternoon."

At this surprising statement Mr. Rizzen-Quicke opened his eyes in astonished remonstrance. "Well, if anybody had tried to persuade me that there was something wrong with your head, Jane, or that you would actually try to make a fool of me, I wouldn't have believed it! Why should I write you a letter when I am never out of your sight above an hour or two at a time? And how could I be in a cab accident when I have been in the house all day? I say, what became of the fat old detective? I must have fallen asleep while I was talking to him." Mrs. Rizzen-Quicke listened to her husband's apparently wild utterances with an awful fear taking shape in her mind, and it was with difficulty that she refrained from crying aloud: "Heaven help us! My poor Joe's brain is turned!" (To be continued.)

div.p: SHE MERELY PICKED IT P.

If Miss E izt Ferridge Lad not taken up a certain newspaper in June, 1895, I should not now tare on my table a letter from her mother, dated in June, 1898— exac' ly thrie pars later. What paper it was, or why Miss Ferridge was moved to read it, we are not told. Probably there was no particular reason why she did it. Her doing it war. an accident,one of the th•n;s that "just happened so." Yet, what do we mein by thtt ? What makes anything "happen "? Heavens ! What bats arid moles we are.

Crossing a piece of strange country one glaemy night, for a short cut, I stumbled over a stone and lamed my- self so badly as to be compelled to seek help at a neigh- b3orlng cabin. There the people congratulated me on what they called limy good luck, saying if I had kept on ten reds longer as I was going, I must have fallen into an abandoned pit,lnd been kilted. On the same lines, I say, if the yourg girl named had not teken up that paper when she did, and found in it what she did, it is more than likely she would not be icing tt.-Jay.

Her mother says E:iza was one a the host of girls who are fated to start out in life without their proper birth- right of vitality. She was weakly and delicate, yet showed no signs of any particular ailment or disease She simply drooped, as flowers do when in an uncon- genial s,il. She complained pf feeling tired and weary, and did not idsy about like other children. However, she got along fairly well—if we may say that of a child who has had no childhood—until she reacheo t re age o fourteen years, when the healthy girl stands, surprised- and blushing, on the deoraill of womanhood. Then her little strength waned and faded until she walked about even more slowly and feebly than befure. 11-!r appetite had always beensmall and capricious, and, if p,ssible, it was less now. Following the poor apologies for meals that Eliza took, came pain in tie stomach, the chest, and elsewhere, as though the hal body ily bore the prrue nee of the food necessary to sustain it.

Seeing this, and justly alarmed by it, Mrs. Ferridg e sought to invigorate the girl by givieg her especially nourishing foods. But no go'd came of it. :The grew more thin and pale, and, if there was red blood Ent' running in her veins, no signs of it showed thrcu;ll her white skin.

In her letter, already alluded to, the mother says : " My anxiety about my daughter's health was at this time very constant and great. She was evidently wast- ing away in spite of all we could do. At this period of her inn( ss sbe was conned to her 13,11 for weeks to- gether. We hid tl help her up and down stairs,and for months I slept in the same room, so as to care fur her in the night.

" She was attended by several doctors, one after another, but none of them had gooi fortune with the case. SuccNsively they gay.) her up, saying they could d) no more. Our friends said Eist WAS in a decline, and no mortal hands could save her. For three years she lingered thus—like one who waits tor a turesummone that may come any day—any hour. "In August, 1893, I got her into Via Convalescent Home at Eastbourne. There she stayed three weeks, at first feeling a trifle bftter far the change, an i then quickly becoming bad as ever. A GIRL'S BEAUTY.

A digtingnished foreigner has well said: "What strikes one most itt Britain is the • lovely complexion of her daughters. The skin , has the bloom of the peach, set off by an indescribable whiteness. which contrasts give a result more admirable than in any other land." Miss Cissie Cowser, a young lady of 15, Palmerston-averne, Clarendon-road, Whalley Range, Manchester, told an interesting history . to a Manchester journalist. She said : " I was always strong and healthy until a little over • , twelve Months ago. Then I began to grow altogether wrong, I felt so weak I could i scarcely manage to walk ; I was always tired— too tired to get about cheerfully. and the sofa was the only desirable place for me. I lost all my colour, my eyes were dim and dull, and I looked dreadful. I wanted the oddest , things to eat—just the things that were worst ' for me. I saw a thoroughly good doctor, but I, still went on in the same way. I had neuralgia dreadfully, the pain in my head being some-- thing indescribable. I could not sleep much, when I did I had terrifying dream& All this j was bad enough, but I suffered in another way— with palpitation of the heart. If I walked quickly or went up stairs my heart beat very fast indeed, the blood pumping, as it were, all through my body. I became very thin, had cold feet always, and, in fact, was cold all over. I took cold, too,. on the slightest exposure.

"Some friends told me about Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People, and I got a box, Before I had finished it, the change was mostl surprising. I felt (I,lferent all over. I took two boxes, and was quite cured. My weariness all left me. I could run about as usual, and my complexion became as right as ever. I cannot tell you bow pleased I was." " And do you remain well ?" "Oh, yes, and I never take cold now; have not had veuralgia for a long time, and the palpitation has all gone. In fact, I am made over again."

Superiatenient FRINIC rGRNER suornitted to the Fire Engine Cornmit;ee his annual redact of fires in Warrington and district fr4c the year ending December, 1898. Toe t3tal number of fires was 26, a decrease 3on thl previous year. There were two serious fires,the remainder being slight. At 12 fir- the brigade's services were not required. The total damage was £21,468, being an increase of £15,765, which was accounted for by the serious fire at the works of Messra. Richmond and Company. The damage outside the borough was £4,100, an increale of -523,340 on the previous 12 months. &gat fires were extinguished by firemen with steam-angines,at 2 they wen assisted with hydrants. The large steamer was used at 1 fire and the small steamer was used at 7 fires. The attendance of firemen had been good.Tne bell rang on 24 encasions, the average attendance being 1715. The men were occupied 283 hours extingu;shing,turning out.and returning from fires, an increase of 191 hours on the previous year, this increase being caused by scarcity of labourers at two large farm fires. Causes of fires :—Unknown 12. defec- tive flues two, timber under hearth one, supposed sparks from engines two, boys smoking one, dropping lighted matches two, boiling ever two, contact with light on?, overheating one, lamp chain braking one, and there was one false alarm. Description of property : Dwelling-houses five, farms nine, chemists one, offices one, engine room one, chip potato shop one, printers one, ropery one, furniture shop one, grocors one, gas engineers showrooms and workshop one, bo ,t shop ONE, stables one. The naonthly practices of the brigade had been well attended. He had inspected tbe fire appliances at the public buildings during toe past year and found them in good condition. EARLESTOWN v. SKERTON. The send round in the Lancashire Junior Cup Com- petition was played off on Saturday, when Ea.riestown, met the cup holders, Skerton, on the home ground. Great interest was taken in the match, by reason of Skerton hay lug defeated Haydeck at the second attempt in the first round, and there was consequently a large gate. Skerton however, had considerably strengthened their teatia,and the eleven they put in the field on Sature• day was their full playing streeeth, whilst Earlestowa were without the assistance of Dewnes. In cons( quence of the recent frost the ground was very hard, arra after play had been in progress some short time it became very slippery. Skerton kicked off and at once invaded the home thretory hut they were driven back, and play was tr resferred to the visitor's quarters. Within a few minutes of the kick off Earlestovra had a good opening and were within an ace of scoring, but Jones cleared' finely. Midfield play ruled for a short time, but the visitors were smarter on the ball, and their combination was finer than that of the home players, and for a con- siderable period they pressed. They could not however lower the Errlrstown colours. The home eleven b 7 a combined rush forced .1-ries to concede a corner,_ but nothing came of the advantage, and Skerton getting away S indersen to k advantage of the opportunity and easily beat Chew. This was rather de- pressiag but the home dower' played strongly and Ilampson getting in a good rosition, shot over tne bar. At half time no further point nad been scored. Sow be- gal to fall, and aided by a strong wind, matters were rendered unpleasant for the home elevea, as they had to face bath snow and wind. They, however, put on some pressure and for some time penned the testcors in their own guar., ra. Final ySi ttle got in, and equalised with, a shot vs h ch gave the custodian n 3 c iance. Tots roused the visftors,but although visits were p kid to each end in rapid success'on, nothing further resulted at the call of time. The match being a draw it was decided to play. an extra half hour,and durin • this period Skerton man- aged to notch two mere goals, thus winning a hard fought game by 3 gcals to 1.

IN the discussions of the ' Unfounded Claims, moment few things have been more amusing than the claims which have) been preferred to inventions and crea::ions. It is a good thing to have new ideas , And new watchwords, and even new leaders, but to ignore history, to assume that tendencies are be- ginning to-day, and tv claim new politics, in disre- gard of old pctiM nd" broad esNnts, is to riaalte, mistake which the ignorant may ridt perdelfq .bLit •tb attired cannot ignore. Three thing S ;laid been efalnio a late that have stuck all middle— aged politicians with surprise. The first is a keen sympathy with our Co7onies and the promotion of federation amongst us. The second is the Im- perial idea, of which claim gir EDWARD GREY ,made such fun the other day. The third is that social politics are worthy of the best attention. If we were to confine our reading to current speeches by Ministers and their champions we should imagine that politics had been a barren business in the days before Mr. CHAMBERLAIN' became Colonial Secretary, Lord SALISBURY waFf. Foreign Minister, and Mr. \. CHAPLIN and Mr. RITCHIE presided over Local Government and Trade affairs. These are, in fact, politics for the young people, who have just begun to dabble in public affairs, after emerging from Board schools and the reading of juvenile publications. The formation of the Dominion of Canada, the crea- tion of new self-governing colonies ut the Cape, and the first germs of Australian Federation were earlier in time than the formation of the Unionist party and the rise of any of its Ministers. The Imperial idea was not unknown in Lord PALMER- STON'S time and earlier. Earl RUSSELL was often animated by it; Mr. GLADSTONE was constantly inspired by it ; Lord ROSEBERY took it up,in some modern forms, when the Colonial Secretary was innocent of any ideas in that direction, and many of his admirers were exulting in narrow and commercial views. The social programme can be found in connection with every Liberal Government that have existed since 1832. It is quite a recent thing for the Conservatives to give it so much prominence. In fact, instead of in- venting it, they stole it, just as they stale Parlia- mentary Reform in 1867. If we were to take out all the social reforms for which we were indebted to the Liberal party, the list would surprise the jejune politicians of to-day. We recommend them to read a little more of our political history before they talk so glibly about new policies, and new ideas, and new partied. The present coalition has the merit of grafting some Libdral ideas upon the old Conservative tree. It is not a permanent process, and it could not be indefinitely carried on The only new thing is the subsidence of Con- servatism ; but it is more apparent than real. The necessity of the moment is thought to be to , keep out Liberalism by presenting a good many limitations of it. To call them new policies is to make an excessive demand upon the credulity of the average human understanding.

International peace projects have our entire ap- proval, but we are none the less sceptical about the proposed limitation of armaments coining to any practical issue. The Peace Conference is to be held at the Hague early. next month, yet its near approach has not the slightest effect pn the un- ceasing augmentation of naval and military forces by all the great powers,mcluJing Russia from whom comes the suggestion of a national disarmament. There are a great many people, with perhaps more confidence in the sense of humanity possessed by their fellow-men than knowledge of the world,who expect great things from the Conference called by the Czar. We fear they are doomed to consider- able disappointment. The fact remains that the great nations of the world are acquiescing in the Czar's humane schemes with one voice and giving orders to their naval engineers and War Depart- ments to develop and expand their forces and re- sources with another. Lord Salisbury himself is not sanguine that the first object of the conference, the arrest of armaments, will be carried out, but with regard to the other two points he is more hopeful. He appears to think that both an extension of the use of arbitra- tion and international legislation for" diminishing the horrors of war" are well within the sphere of practical European politics. If the conference ac- complishes even as much as the Prime Minister is prepared to anticipate it will have done a good work, but that it will effect any reduction in arma- ments whatever we do not believe. The Armaged- don which many authorities are convinced is advancing will, if it should come, do more in this direction than any scheme that a peace conference can devise.

The future of the Manchester Ship Canal is as- sured. It has already outlived the prophecies of its failure ; it has secured for itself a considerable portion of the commerce of the world; it has de- monstrated to all and sundry its ability to accommo- date cargo vessels of the largest and most modern class ; it has for some time been able to pay all its workin;! ; ani it has now begun to pay

• interest on the Manchester Corporation loan of £5,000,000. Such facts as these engender an un- shakable confidence in the ultimate success of the great undertaking. The present outlook is bright in the extreme—perhaps not for the original share- holders, who ought to be, if they are not already, resigned to their fate—and there is every reason to hope and believe that the Ship Canal Company will in course of time become a paying concern and a lasting monument to Lancashire commercial ,enterprise. Along with the gradual but continu- ous development of Ship Canal resources will in. • evitably come widespread prosperity, in which even those who have come to be regarded as the bitterest opponents of the undertaking must of necessity participate.

A number of meetings in support of the Inter- national Crusade of Peace have been held up and clown the country during the course' of the past *week, and this circumstance has perhaps had something to do with the sudden ebullition of lo- cal interest in the subject. We do not suggest that the interest has only just sprung into life because we are aware that the opposite is the case,but until last week nothing had been done towards elicit- ing the opinion of the inhabitants of Warrington .on this important subject. Last week, how- ever, a number of prominent townsmen met to- gether and subsequently requested the Mayor to call a town's meeting, and his Worship readily consented with the result that on February 20th the requisite opportunity will be afforded the townspeople of expressing their views. We hardly need urge the importance of some scheme for the restriction of national armaments—it is patent to everyone—for at present the expenditure on the munitions of war by the different nations, and this country in particular, is bounuless. From consi- deratians both of economy and humanity some- thing should be done, and the young Emperor of Russia has led the way in a fashion which has evoked universal commendation. The daily papers just now contain nearly as much about French submarine schemes as about peace proposals, but this contradictory state of things should only be a greater incentive to the Warrington public to attend the meeting and express their opinions with unquestionable decisiveness.

On Tue9day evening the teachers of the Sunday school's held in connection with the Trinity Chuicb and Mariners Mission, sat down to their annual tea at the Mariners' Mission schoolroom. DEATH 010 N 111,4 QUECKETT. The death of Mrs. Queckett took place on Tues- day afternoon, at a quarter to four, at her residence in Eccleston-square, Loudon. The deceased lady was the widow of the Rev. William Queckett, for many years Rector of Warrington, who died at the Rectory on Good Friday, 1888, being succeeded by the present Rector, the Rev Canon Willis. Mrs. Queckett's sou, Mr. R. G. Wehstar, is M.P., for East !-it. Pancras. Mrs Queckett who had reached a good age, was the eldest sister of Colonel Hodgson, who served with distinction throughout the Cabal Cam- paign in 1842, and was engaged in actions in January, 19, 23, and 24, at the entrance to the Khy- ber Pass, and at the forcing of it on April sth, 1842. Mrs Queckett was on a visit to the Warringtou Rectory about three or four years ago, when she ' was taken suddeely ill while in church. She re- maintd in a critical condition for several days, but ultimately recovered, and returned to London.

WESLEYAN CHAPEL.—The annual Sunday school and creational tea meeting and prize distribution in con- neclen with the Wee !even Chapel took place on Tues- day. There was a good atteilance at the tea, and at the public meeting afterwards the room was well filled. Mr. Strnusl Moss presided. An exc Ilnt entertainment was provided, the programme consisting of music and recitatiens, rendered chiefly by juvenile scholars. Miss Edo Miller proved herself an acceptable accompanist to her young friends. The report of the past year's work in the Sunday school was read by the Secre- tary, Mr. H. Brcreton. Gool progress had been made during the year and the outlook was encouraging and hopeful. The attendanse boqi of sell-Alm and teachers was satisfactory, though there was a need for mo; e workers. The number of prizes awarded to scholars for punctuality was 51. The various departments were in goed vrrking order. The Juvenile Club was well established, and was being efficiently maintained, as was also the Penny Bank, into the funds of which £l2 had bean paid during the year. Temperance work was also kept up, the Band of Rope holding a rezular weekly meeting which was well attended, and a Javenile 11,chabite Tent was also being conducted with success. Their most pressing need was Utter school accommodation, the teaching having to be carried on under ditficulties.—The Rev. G. Harbottle, in addition to d s4ribeting the prizes, delivered an interest- ing address. Messrs. S. B. Stringer and R. Miller having spoken, the Rev. J. S. Hughes, of Hill Cliffe, addressed the meeting. Mr. W. Goslin contributed a recitation entitled " The Deaeon's Meeting." A vote of thanks to all whsi hai assisted in the entertainment was passed on the proposition of Mr. A. H. Dunn, seconded by Mr. , John Miller.

They took, he said, the words of the text that night and used them as their own. They were as appropriate to them in War- rington as they were when uttered away beyond Jordan. They were meant for all time, for His words should never pass a way. Their friead Mr. Lees was fallen ' asleep. A violin s:1) was effic.d t,tl,e given by Mr. Thomas eValliagten, Mr. Payton a."'"Y ' peuying on the oreari. ccom- END OF THE WORLD. In the absence of Mr. Briggs of Sowerhy Bridge through sickness, Mr. G. Waite of .Wigan lectured en the above suoject on Suuday in the .Christadelphia Boom, Bold-streec. He said thet there were definite signs of the times in regard to the subjecr, of his lecture,which it was a misfortune not to know about, and a crime Ireovving of them, they were ignored or neglected. The nature of the time an' its relationseip to Christ's com- ing must be looked for in the political, rather than the natural heaven. Many expected natural signs to precede the coming ot Curist, but if they considered the pro- phecies with regard to God's judgments on Jerusalem tney would find coat political events were predicted to occdr, which did occur,before the overthrow of that city and similarly pelitical events had occurred, which warned them now,of the near approach ot the end of the times of the Gentiles. The lecturer proceeded to e stab- nab his position by a critical analys s and comparison of the terms used in the 13. h Caketer of Isaish, wherein the words heaven, earth, sun, moon, and stars, are used politically, respecting the Babylonian Kingdom, and had ; no reference whatever to the natural heaven and earth, Etc. There were to be social and political upheavals pre- I eeeding the end of this age, but there was not any language in tare Bible justifying the idea that the earth (natural) Was to be burned up, and it teey examined csretully the fire mentioned by Peter in the light of what he had said they would see how much it had been misrepresented; for while tee earth was t be burned up the heavens also w. 71•8 to past away. Tee prediction was political not natural, as was shown by the preceding references to the earth perisbieg, &s. Touching on the colossal image of Daniel ansl the stone Which destroyed it,Mr.Waite showed that the image was emblematic of the several dynasties indicated by the different metels of which the image was composed, and that the oestroying stone represented Christ, who after he had overthrewn the Kingdoms of this world, would t up a kingdom which should never be destroyed. Though they could net tell Vete day nor hour when that much desired event would be, many political events (several being given particularly) showed they were rapidly approacning that epoch. There was a good attendance, and the lecture was listened to with marked attentlion throagheut. THE LATE DR. BERRY. MEyrORIAL SERVICE IN WYCLIFFE CHURCH. Thorp was a large congregation in Wycliffe Congrega- tiegol Chuych, Warrineton, on Sunday evening whcu a memprial service for the late Rev. C. A. Berry, D.D., of Weivernereptem, was held The Bev. Jetta Yonge was the preacher, and ho selected for his text the words These are they who Caine out, of great tribulation, and have washed her robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. Teerefore are they beforethe Throne of God, end serve idem day and night in His Temple" (Rev: vii. 14-15). It hid, the preacher said, been stated that these words were the text of the first sermon ever preached by Dr. Charles Albert Berry, whose death was now Call9lOg such widespread sorrow in thezr churches ; and they who knew anything of the character of his life- long ministry would know that the sublime truths either declared or implied in that ton hal ever been the staple of his preaching. And now they were in the presence ef the fact that by a startlingly sudden transition he had been himself ushered into the glorified assembly, was himself now numbered with the great host "before the Throne and before the Lamb." Thus what had been the subject of his glowing faith and often of his eloquent imagination had become the Obj,C; of his enraptured sight. At this rnoment,he was " before the Throne of Clot" How abstlutely trans- Icending all thought and speech must have !pen tile apocalypse which dawned upon i 3 Spirit in that eils prense moment when in the very midst of an act of earthly ministry,he saw hie Master face to face. To the church on earth, to his large circle of friends, to his hmity, he now remained as a memorvi hut a Meenary full of stimulating infitlenoe thi quickening power. The Christian public, of course, had only known Dr. Berry as a Christian nahtister of large capacity, of popular gift and powerful speech. As such be had became known even in Wycliffe Church, for be had stood in. tit palpit both on Sunday and on week day, and they had felt the force and living fervour of his clear enuncialon of truth of his "ft in prayer, and his eloquence both Of word and eeider,eta Tir typ churches at Bolton and Wele.erhamp- ton, which lied Aare Detween them the term of his public minietry, united le i•fitll2l3" as to the marvel- 4:ha af tdech- letle force of his persoeality and fidey o ing. He had died at 46 years of age, an... bis 1111an..st"YI therefore, had been but comparatively brief. tia minister in their denomination, so far as be knew, had in their time at least, been so conspicuously slice nsful, and none had been more universally lamented. He (Mr. 'rouge), remembered the beginning of his career, when Dr. Berry settled as pastor of Ste George's reed Congre- ! gational Church, Bolton. Circumstances often occurred which brought them into contact, and when he entered, as he did very quickly, into the denominational work of the county, and became a member of the Union Execu- tive, then intimacy rapidly grew. Be soon developed conspicuous -talent for affairs, being quick to realise a Situation, accurate in solving difficult problems of „publie duty able to conciliate and manage awkward and eitireal affairs, earnest and resolute and untefish in all thee. eavoured of duty. His capacity for the work of his church Wee prophecy of hisepapacity for the wider ser- vice of the country, and as a leader of the whole denominatiort be bad won the confidence of all his brethren and of all the Churches. It was the tact and courage he displayed in a season of crisis in one of their larger denominational gatherings that carried him forward to the threshold of a career which, had he accep- ted it, would have enriched Ameeca at the cost of this country. Believing that; the late Henry Ward Beecher, on a visit to this country, was experiencing unfair treat- ment at the hands of some, Dr. Berry came to the rescue of the situation, by courtesy, tact, and courage concilia- ting all, and gratifying intensely the man whose cause he championed. Out of that incident came the ether in which Beecher confided to a friend that he believed that Berry was the man who should succeed him at Brooklyn when his day was done. They remembered how the event issued, and Beery was callei upon to occupy that great sphere in Brooklyn where Beecher had lived and laboured with such world wide influence and force. Most people in this country took it for granted that Mr. Berry would accept the call. Newspapers— and even one in this town, declared that as the proffered etipend was far in excess of what Mr. Berry was receiv- ing here,he wonld be sure to see in that a "providential indication." Mee of the world did cceasionally judge other men exclusively by their own bushel, and they did so then. With a tranquil modesty, but a resolute firmness Mr. Berry declined the call, and from that time and that act ho became one of the greatest forces in their Congregational body, a recognized and trusted leader, a preacher whose services were sought on every band. And be gave himself to the general service of the denomination with an ardour and enthusiasm which had no doubt unhappily conspired to develop his malady and shorten his days. He wanted to say in Dr. Berry's honour that however some men might have been careful to make popularity a channel of personal emolument, that was never his bent at all. He had served the Denomination at considerable personal sacrifice, not only of time and strength, but even of money also. He did net travel the country thorough merely to " star " it and to create a personal fArle. He believed that be had a distinct work to do for Christ among our churches,and his people shared his belief to do thae work was the passionate wish of his whole life. Dr. Berry was a man after the type of Dr. Dale. He believed, and rightleolthat the Congregational idea was the very highest idea of Christ's church, because it made the church the authority, it recognised it as a vr ritible divine society—the com- pany of believers being ever presided over and con- trolled, if they be faithful and true to the great head of the church. It was to expound this that Dr. Berry

ilaboured specially in recent years; and he himself told him (sir. Yonge) that he had even seriously considered whether he would not abandon the pastorate, and take up a crusade througheut the denomination, for the assertion of the true nature and Divine function& of the company of believers. Tbis theme was dear to his heart. It was often the staple of nii conversations. This led him to say that Dr. Berry was one of the most brilli- ant conversationalists and his talk was always of a true and high level. lie should ever count it one of the great privileges of his life that he could count Dr. Berry as an iatimate triend, and words failed him to say how deeply he deplored his premature thpartura. Of all men he ever knew Dr. Charles Berry was the most completely brotherly. And here the testimony was . unanimous, both among ministers and laymen. Such success as he achieve I would have placed many a man on sucn a lofty pinnacle that he would become unap- proachable. Not so that man. He was the same Charles Berry, frank, friendly, loving, loyal from stu- dent to president. They were at home with him in- stantly. Not to love that in in, if they knew him, was to demonstrate the poverty of their own power t) love. And now " we shall see his face no wore" on this aide the ruler. The news came upan them with overwhelming power. How tragic, and yet, as had been fi-.ly said, bow ideal, for for him was the manner el ha departure l He had gone b kck t) work with the new year, not because his ad- visers deemed hint capable, but because they thought the strain of inactivity might be more dangtroas than the strain of service. He had preached °ace on each Suriday in January, and on Tuesday last, having mar- ried a couple in the forenoon, he went in the afternoon to bury his medical attendant and personal friend. Pray- ing for his friend's widow, he suddenly fell upon the .floor of the rostrum of the church, and instantly ex- pired. There and then his ministry was endei, and his seirit passed to its celestial rest and reward. That "elo- quent tongue" was uttering its Last; and was now for ever in this sphere, Eileut in the grave. Tuough his body had fallen WAS not his spirit marching on. " Taanks be unto God who has given him the victory through Jesus Ceris; our Lord." "lie is before tte Throne of God,and serves Him thy and night in His Temple." at the close the choir aave an effective rendering of the anthem "These are they."

White, solicitor, who appeared to prosecate, said the case bad been adjourned from the Warrington County Petty Sessions to give defendants an opportunity of appearing to answer the charge, but they hid absconded. The offence was that of being on land at night time with a gun for the purpoie of taking game. Abut 10.30 on Saturday, the 21st January, George R )bert Leigh, a gainekeaper, was on duty near Bewssy Park and heard Pveral shots fired, and want towards Bewsey locks where be hid himsfrlf to intercept them. After a few minup: a he saw both defendants come along a fi-ld skirting a plantation known as the pock Plantation, which was a far place for phesiants roosting. Roberts bad a gun, and Handley's pockets wac bulky.i..igh ran Vtat and se7zed hold of Roberts, but Handley ran up and pushed him off, and they both ran away. Leigh called out to them that it was no use them running away as he knew them. rh3 off mce,.
