The death of the Hereditary Prity:e of Saxc-Coturg- Gotta, is a sad ending to the silver wedding festivities ot his parents,who adored him. Be was the eld,?tt child and only son, the other four children of the Duke and Duchess of Saxe-Coburg-Gottia being,the Crown Princess of R3umania, the Grand Duchess of HeSEC, the Heredi- tary Princess of Hohenlohe-Langenburg, and the youth- ful Princess Beatrice. The Grand Duchess of Hesse will feel the loss of her brother keenly. She was his favourite sister, and the two had been the firmest friends from their earli(st days. Treubles seem to have fal!en thick and fast upon the Duchess of Saxe-Coburg of late yea's. The late Prince's health caused her almost ceaseless anxiety, al!cl that of the Duke c.nisderable uneasiness, some time ago. Then her daughter's matrimonial differences have been no small anxiety. And now comes the loss of lier only,and dearly-loved son, a blow, those who know the Duchess well, declare she will utver fully recover from. The Queen of the Belgians is still cancelling her en- gagements, ( wing to an attack of influenza, from which she has recovered but slowly. Riding and dtiving are still the Queen's chief pleasures, and when driving her- self, is always seen in a lightly-hung rony carriage, drawn by four hots3s. These horses, which came from a special Hungarian breed, are all bred and broken at Lacken, in the Royal stables, and stud farm, and till lately the Qlccn often tcok active part in the training of her hot ses.

Married at seventeen to the youthful, then Duke of Brant, she became a Que(n at thirty, an-I the reign opened prosperously. Fortune seemed to firmer her lavcurs on the Royal pair, until their only son, an in- telligent little lad of ten, died suddenly. From this shock, the Queen of the Belgians may be said, never to have recovered. The anniversary ot her son's death, is kept by her each year in deep seclusion, and his name is never mentioned.

The birth of a lion and heir to Lord and Laely Setring- ton has cause I great rejoicing in the fain iye Their other son, it will be remembered died in intaucy, to the great grief of his pareats. There is a custom in the family of the Duke of Richmond, which amounts to law —through its antiquity—that eldest sons, grat daons, and great grandsons of the !armee, shall be christened Charles after the founder Charles 11, therefore the new baby will in future be known as the Hon. Charles Gordoe-Lennox• The great grandson of a living duke I; a somewhat rare personage. During the past ten pare or so, no fewer than 152 American women have married European noblemen,and the dowries they have brought amount in the aggregate to rather more than £3,330,000. An American journal has recently been asking its feminine readers,why Ameri- can girls are Si fono of titles. One of the hetet known and most travelled women in New York society says she can only explain on the assumption that the United States has no titles of its own, and that things cistant and unknown alway; seem to be of greater value than those with which we are familiar. But most of the letters admit more or less frankly, that it is pure vanity, love of adulation, and of an assured position in Europe that brings about these ama!gamations of wealth and nobility. Miss Olga Nethersnle, who, upon her return from America will open at a West-end London th atre, is of Spanish descent, her great grandmother having been of pure Castilian birth. She has been on the stage about eleven or twelve years, having made her debut when she was eighteen, at the Theatre Royal, Brignten. The greatest American triumphs of Miss Nethereole were in Freu-Frou, La Dame aux Camillias. and Romeo and Juliet. Juliet, she says, is to be the first part she will essay when she produces Shakespeare in London, as she hopes to do shortly. Only the very best materials are used nowadays for theatrical gowns, and many titled women would bo glad enough to have relveseelkstlanct laces, of such a quality as leading actress-s often toed b tt: in the dust of ,:he stage. Frequently as much as 12 guineas is given a yard for velvet. and 10 guirreal a yard for brocaded si3e. The latter was paid quite Weis by a Viennese actress, the whole costume costing EIEO. There is a growing teed- ency towards extravagance in this respect. In erdinary life, much more money is spent than formerly on dress, and public taste is all for gorgeous spectacle in ballet, and pantomino, and realism—accuracy of costume and mounting—in the drama. Fashionable women stern to grow thinner and thinner as time goes on. How they accomplish the feat is some- thing of a mystery, but of course the cut of their under garments, arid corsets, have a little to do with the &- sired result. All uneecessary fulness is dispensed with. If underskirts are worn, they are buttoned on to the edge of the corsets, not; carried up to the waist. Slip bodices are sloped away after fastening over the bust, and el not reach to the waist. In the size of ones hips and waist, these arrangements make a gnat difference, and in practising such arts we certainly have the satis- faction of knewing them to be harmless. in hats, the general shape for srme time past has been I flat, and rather wide, but with the spring we are to alter this. High crowns will be cermet, which will Ee7p to' give height. The tailer and slimmer we can make our selves appear, the more up-to-date ehall we be considered and a large brim and high crown adorned w;tn long plumes will certainly aid us in this matter. _

The cravat is in high favour, and promises to continue E 0 for come time to come. Sometimes it is made of sffir ternetimes of mirror velvet, and it is worn with fronts, shitts, and boeices. Regarding the collars of our gowns. these can scarcely hava too much attention bestowed upon them. The most becoming perhaps are those that stand slightly away from the neck at the back, and slope towards the front, the lining being of lace, or deli- cately tinted chiffon. Others have a point rising under each ear, the edge being softened with a ruche of lace or chiffon. These can be made separate if preferred, and fastened with neat hooks and eyes. l'ar;sian omen, according to a French paper just to band are almost as fond nowadays of a five o'clock cup of tea as we are! Many tea rooms it seems. now exis- in leading thoroughfares, and the sale of tea ic Paris has trebled during the last twelve years. Judging from what a medical journal has to say concerning the taking of our tea in the form of cigarette', this particular vice will not fisurish long. The first sensation it says, though peculiar, is Lot unpleasant, but a disposition to take hold of something, or sit down, quickly follows, and if the novice perseveres the after effects are fre- quently such, that it takes her some hours to revive. Fencing among growing girls is a favourite pastime and bids fair to become shortly, equally popular atnon g those sho have passed tne growing stage. That the exercise tends to call forth strength and grace, there can be no possible doubt, and the danzer is minimised to the least possible chance, as guards for the face and chest are deemed absolutely indispensable. The ordinary dress adopted for this amusement, is that of the gymna- sium, consisting of a loose shirt, and skirts of serge in any colour. GATEAU OF APPLMS.—In a quart of water boil three pounds of loaf sugar till it becomes a thick syrup. Then core and peel four pounds of good cooking apples, and add to the syrup. Squeeze in the juice of three lemons, and boil all together till nearly a paste. Pour into moulds, and when cold turn out a solid jelly. Snwed with boilei custard. Tots makes a very pretty dish.

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
MY DEAR_NELLIE,

It is really impossible just now to give a Ratios factory answer to your question as to the spring fashions. It is yet too early. All that I can say just now is that coats and skirts are the proper wear. In all tailor•made costumes the coats are short, have semi fitting fronts, revers, and sleeve minus cuff,. A particularly chic efftir is of Russian blue cloth, the skirt biaidsd just below the knees with narrow blue cord fl.,eked with gold. The /it tie coatee is outlined with this blue and 4old cord, and froge of it decorate the trout, lueyes and

I recently saw a charming beaver hat with natural ostrich feather., Hnd 1.1)1qa.,,5e velvet, fattened in front with a handsome steel ornament. This and the natural ostrich boa is very becoming. So far as hats in ordinary are omeerned the picture variety remains, ()illy chaeg- ing its uontour and trimming in aascordance with the prey tiling modes. There is so ill a defieire feeling iii tnyour of ire or LFN 0 shades of a single celour, forming the make•up" of a hat, and a p et ure shipe of this kind if it is to be worn in the street is very nimeh more appropriaLely trimmed in such a way. so that in g.nerai effect it may be quiet but at the same time halel:•oine. For tio-i moment feather sod fur ;agues carry all before them, and ceri airily grebe oyed to the required chta is is far prettier than clinehilla and more be- coming to the complexion. White toques trimmed with gardenias and dark green leaves, with a dash of colour at the side, are the newest thing, and tnques made entirely of (Prise tinted feathers, with a keot of velvet to match, are finding a great deal of favour.

A bodice sir had pointed out to me the other day was of soft silk, drawn into folds, and fastening on the left side. Sailor collar and revers edged with gathered ribbon or lace. Small under vest of embroidery. Tight sleeves, with one side set in small tucks or pipings. You will be enabled, perhaps, from this brief duscription to in some measure judge of the effect produced.

In regard to evening gowns, bright bizarre colourings have given way to the daintiest of pale, soft tints, which fitly harmonise with fragile laces and ethereal tulle and chiffon. Full dress gowns are invariably made with the shoulder-strap crossing the shoulder, and the sleeve starting low on the arm, leaving the rounded top of the arm exposed. The quaint touch of black which is so exceedingly fasnionable, appears even on the lightest gowns. Sometimes it is a mere line of black running amongst soft lace or dividing hand- some passementerie, but a scarf of black chiffon draped across the bust, or rosettes or loops of black chiffon or velvet, fastening portions of the bodices, or figuring as Empire knots to connect tabs or draperies, is its most effective form. White silk stitching on cloth gowns is rapidly coming into favour with the members of our sex in town, and it is expected to be quite übiquitous as spring advances. A charming example which I saw lately was made of fawn cloth, the skirt machined with a double row of white silk, be- tween which small gold buttoos were set in groups of three. The bodice was in semi-military style, with white cloth facings and strappings, and more gold buttons, and the yoke or cape was tritnmed with white silk cords attached to very small gold Imam's. The vest or waistcoat was quite plain except for rows of white stitching. Some of the prettiest silks for evening wear have white grounds with coloured stripes, and tiny flowers between them in na`otral tones. 'When these are trimmed with chiffon and lace -atter the picturesque style of the Georgian period they certainly have a very great success. In draughty passages the new evening boas are likely to be warmly appreciated, for they add to the appearance and are certainly warm. They are toads of lace, trimmed with ribbons or embroidered in black and colours ; sometimes they are entirely cootoosed of rose petals, and marabout is utilised for them, as also for evening capes. To revert for a moment to dress proper, let me say that I have noticed that not only are small blossoms and their green foliage popular, but cloth, velvet, and satin in the same tints bid fair to be all the rage. Already about every fourth woman in the West-end streets or in the Park wears a costume of more or less vivid violet. The bluish shades sawn to be preferred, and they certainly wear better than the red ones, and look better too in the sunshine when it deigns to visit us. Almond-coloured cloth is sometimes com- bined with violet velvet, but green dresses are to be quite out of the running for some months to come.
Your loving JENNII

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. HOUSE O- F LORDS. THE QUEE- N'S SPEECH.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. HOUSE O- F LORDS. THE QUEE- N'S SPEECH.

The fifth session of the fourteenth Parliament of the Queen was opened on Tuesday, by Commii,sioa in the House of Loris. The Queen's Speech, which was read by the LORD CHANCELLOR, opened with the statement that relations with other Powers centinued friendly. Reference was then made to the Soudan txpedition and to the appointment of Prince George of Greece as Governor of Crete. The Tsar's Rescript was next spoken of. The Queen had gladly signified her wiliingoess to take part in the deliberations of the Conference " to. consider the possibility of limiting the vast arma- ments which impose so heavy a burden on every nation." The murder of the Austrian Empress and the recent Conference in Rome upon Anarchism were touched upon, and it was stated that some amendment of the law in reference to the latter subject would be submitted for the conside:ation of Parliament. The Speech then alluded to the West Indian hurricanes,after which came an expresstcn of great satisfac:ion at the Cape contribution ot the navy. The first part of the Speech concluded with a reference to the plague in India. With regard to domestic legislation, the Speech gave the first and second places to a Bill " for more fully orgaicising the government of the metro- polis" and a Bill for the establiihment of a " board fo r the administration of primary, seconcitry, and technical education. Some ten other measures were mentimei.

The business sitting of the House of Lords commenced at a quarter-past four, when the DUKE of BEDFORD moved and the EARL of CAWDOR sec mded the Address in reply to the speech from the Throne. The EARL Of KIMBERLEY followed, and in the course of his criticism of the contents of the Royal Speech said he could not but regard the question of our position in the Soudan as an import ant and grave matter, and owned that he was a little perplexed by the allusion to the complete sub- jogati;.n of the territories which had been brought under the dominion of the Khalifa. He gathered that if these territories had rot been completely subjugated, it was the policy of the Government to complete that work. The announcement that the Soudan had been taken pos- session of in the names of her MAJESTY and of the KHE- DIVE sermed to him to be fraught with very far reaching consequences. What must be meant, he thought, was that we had practically made the Soudan a pert of the British Empire ; and the assumption of so huge a terri- tory involved re ponsibilities or a very serious nature, especially in regard to the troops by whom order was to be pr.,served. As regarded China, he pressed the Government to give • the country full infor- mation as to the present condition of affairs, and as to the policy they intended to pursue.— The MARQUIS of SALISBURY replying, said as to the use of the word subjugation with reference to the Soudan, subjugation was used in the ordinary sense—that was to say. we had conquered the political power by which these territories were held, had seizsd the capital, and were administering the affairs of the country with a view of bringing it into a condition of security: He did not thirk that the strain upon the British Army would be at all severe. As to the policy of the Govern- ment in Claire, thP future of that country did not lie in our bands. The Government would see that treaties were faithfully carried out, and that rothing was done by China or other nations which could interfere with cur rights. Our policy there was to promote the trade of this coontry ; and to suppose that we were contem- plating the acquirement of territory in China was ab- surd.—Lord STANMORE having added a few words, the Addrets was agreed to, the Earl of Morley was reap- pointed Chairman of Committees, and the House ad- j mrned at ton minutes past six.

div.head: "THE TRurii ABOUC 031DURNIAN."
div.p: "THE TRurii ABOUC 031DURNIAN."

Sir,—lt will doubtless be iii the recollection of your readers, that after the terrible carnage at Omdurman a Thanksgiving Service was held on the field of betties. Surrounded by thousands of awfully mangled and dead bodies of men and animals, and with their ears pierced with the agonising cries of the weunded, whose blood crimsoned the ground, three preachers of the Gospel were found fit and willing to " perform " the gruesome ceremony. I dare not dwell even for a little on this strange proceeding ;it ie. too revolting for anyone who has the humble,t conception of the merciful and gracious being whom we call God. But as one of the actors in the scene has appeared in the press as an apologist for the killing of the wounded dervishes which Newspaper Correspondents allege took place after the victory, I will devote a few remarks to his apology. In a letter under the above heading published in the "Methodist Times" and reproduced in the "Manchester Guardian "of the 3rd inst., Mr. 0.5. Watkine,Wesleyan Chaplain to the forces on the Nile says," With regard to the order issued (by the Sirdar I presume) previous to the halle, which I understand Mr. Bennett to say was a command te iill all wounded dervishes—l have not kept a copy of that order—bur, as my memory serves me,it was to the effect that all dingerous wounded were ta be at once killed." That is to say the poor half- armed children of the desert who were not deprived of life by the Maxims,Gatlings and other approved weapons of Christendom, but were laid weltering in their blood on the burning sand, were to be finished off by the bayonet lest in their death struggle they should prove daneerous to the heroes of the d iy. Again, the Method- ist MAO tin says, "At Omdurman I saw many wounded men killed," but excises the killing on the ground that the victims " were all showing fight," and indignimtly ask 3 "was it brutal to kill such men." But this is not all. With a fine gush of patriotiim the Methodist Chaplain Vames those who make chirps of cruelty againa the brave fellows who performed the wotk " in the waste Soudan for Queen and Country." I fear Mr. 0. S. Watkins, like many others has mis- taken his calling : he shou'd be a Minister others, Sword and not of the Cross. The cruel, vindictive spirit which breathes through his letter is about as different to the spirit of Christ as hell ie to heaven. Jesus came not into the world "to destroy men's lives, but to save them" ; and to his followers he left such instructions as these, " I sty unto you, that ye resiet no; evil : but whosoever shall smite thre on thy right cheek, turn t ) him the other also." " Leve your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to tnetn that hate you, and pray for them that despitefully use you, and perse- cute you." And then, to erriona.sise this blessed and loving teaching He Himself prayed for Hie murderers when they were nailing Him to the Cross. In the light of all this how horrible must the war in the Soudae appear to minds not led astray by the maxims of the world. If JE sus is to be regarded as our exemplar it seems to me that under no circumstances whatever is it lawful forCbristian men t) imbrue their hands in the blood of their fellow creatures. All the talk that one hears in the pulpit and elsewhere about just wars, self defence &c , is only another development of peer hum an nature.—Yours tru'y, lONA.
WARRINGTON CORE'ORA.TION BILL.

Sir,—Yeur correspondent " lona,'" is not a careful man, or tie would before rushing into print have assured himself that the statements he m tde in his letter of Saturday last were really accurate As a matter of fact he has been grossly misinformed upon both the points which be has attempted to ventilate. The proposals for the " Thrift Fend " are intended specifically for the benefit of the tool-leave employed in the various depart- ments of the Corporation, and taoee offi3ial3 who are " well paid for their work" are to be entirely excluded. That this" Tnrift Fund" would ultimately be a decided benefit to the ratepayers I am confident and for this reason. At the present moment in one department alone there are nearly a dozen Men who have grown old in the town's service having b sea employed in their present capacities for potiods of from 20 to over 30 years each. They are not now and have not been for some time pint earning the full amount of the wages they rec iive simply because the natural decay of their physical powers has made it imposeinle for them to do so. The Committee under whom these men are employed feel that if they were discharged, the only place of re- fuge for most of them would be the Workhouseond they naturally shrink from forcing old and faith- ful servants, however bumble, into such a humiliatieg and painful posit' in. In other words these men are now partially pensioners on the rates of the borough. Is it not therefore is "penny wise and le nand foolish "policy to keep up the present conditions when the estahlishment of a thrift fund to which all the pos- sible beneficiaries would centribate weekly, would, act- ing autematically,place these men at a certain ago upon a properly managed pension list. I don't think it takes a great deal of discernment or business capability to ap- preciate tho cemmonseaso character of this propomT. IL Now as to" "second paint. I aeree in the first place with every word he Faye as to th, moral and reli- gious iniquity of the enforcement of banal fees, but at the SAM time these charees so far as the clergy of the Church of England are concerned are legalised and can- not be got rid of except by purchase or legislation. What is it that the bill proposes to do? The conditions which at present obtain are them. As a rule the burial ser- vice of Nonconformists is conducted by Nonconformist ministers, and te their honour be it said there are innu- merable instances in which they perform this duty without any money, payment whatever, but in every in- stance a fee has to be paid by the relatives to the c'er,gymen of the parish, in which the &c eased previously resided. It is with the objc.ct of getting rid for ever of this injus- tice,which is one of the remnants of clerical avarice and nviaich is neither more nor lens than a legalised plunder- frig of Nenconfermist citizons, that it is proposed in th 3 Bill to take power to commute the life interests of the present holders of these unearned emoluments. I have no doubt whatever that when this matter is fully under- stood that sense of justice arnl f iirplay which I *tOgWa is characteristic of the great bulk of my fellow towns- -tan will cause them to support nis just and wise pro- posal. The Corporatica Bill is a Tooel sound melSure ad Oge which if passed into law will de mach to improta out town and to proreole the centinuous and growing pros- perity of our citizens. Ido not for a moment believe that it will throw any serious burden upon the rates,bat on the other hand by a judicious provision for an in. creased supply of that element weich is so essentially necessary to the comfort, health, and life of our peop7e and to the continued development of our commercial un- dertakings, it will in a very few years secure a source of increasing revenue which may be applied to any purpose of public utility within the cQqtrol ef the Coueeil.—l am, yews faithfully,
RENRV ROBERTS.

Sir,--1 am sufficiently well acquainted with the Mayor te be cenvinced he has no wish except to do the host that can possibly be done for the town, and that he has no intention to mislead your readers. His letter, which appeared in your last IESIII, she ws that he must have been seriously micaformad, and this, I nope you wilt allow me to prove, without importing any personal feeling into the diecussioe. Mylast letter was intended to point out that the Bold water scheme had not received adequate attentien at the bands of the Corporation, becau-e th-y were under the impression the supply might be only temporary. Toe Mayor has confirmed me. Ho states :—" I do not wish to infer for one memen-, that the water at Bold Colliery is not likely to be as p-rmanent as at Winwick. That is not the point. The Bold Hall Colliery is a business speculation, and a supply frem that source would be in the eon*rol of the owners of the colliery. What guaran- tee would the C_rporation have that the owners for financial or other reasons might not close the works ?" Tnis statement would be perfectly true and reasonable if we were a mere colliery company working under ordinary colliery leases ; but the Mayor must have for- gotten a conversation 1 had with him upon this very question. I told him that we were actual freehold owners of the Bold Estate, not rrr.re lessees, and conse- quently we could give the Corporation power to enter and work the pumps themselves, should we fail to do so—of course deducting the expense from the water rents payable to the company. He replied that this re- moved this great difficulty. Upon the point, therefore, of the permanency of the supply from Bold I taink there can be no reasonable doubt, and it must be remembered that we are now actually pumping over 3,000,000 gaPoes rer day, whilst at Winwick the new sinking's alight or might not be a success, and in any case it has not even been suggested that the supply would b 3 increased by more than about 11 million gallons per day. The next point made by the Mayor in his letter is as to the quality of the Bold water, and here he has fallen into a very startling error. He states the Winwick water has eleven cl: grees of harness as against Bold water 21 deerels and that the latter is without treat- ment unfit for domestic or manufacturing purpo;e3. The best answer I can give to this statement is to copy the analyses that have been made of the two waters :- --
EXTRACTS FROM ANALYSES. Bold Winwick Water. Water. Hardness temporary 14.0 11.6 Permanent

Total 21.5 21 2 The analyst goes on to El HardnesP practically the same." . . . "Speaking generally the B)Id water id the same type as the Winwick." I cannot imagine how the Mayor can have obtained his figures, unless he has compared the temporary hardness of NN in- wick with the total hardne3s of Bold. Then as to Bold water being " withcut treatment unfit for domestic or raanufazturiag purposes ", let us see

what Mr. Deis, the Warrington water engineer, rays abmit it. I have a report signed by him in wbich says : "This water (from Bold) is organically very pure, and as such would be well fitted tor household pur- poreL It is, however, very hard." I have also another certificate from an eminent cl2et:iiit who states : " I consider this water as a good 11,4Ithy water which can be used for c)nsutnption purposes." All this proves wtat 11 stated in my previous letter, that the water from Bold and that from Winwiek are practically identical in quality. They ara both very pure and healthy waters, but hard.

Upon the question of the cost of bringing Bold water to Warrington. I statel that a 12in. main capable of de- livering one and a half million gallons per day could be laid down for £2,000 per mile, at which price I know a contract has been let.

Tho Mayor does not question this, but says that th.v would put down a 27,n. main at a cost of £3l-926. Now a 271 n. main has a capacity of deliver- ing over 7,000,000 gallons per day with sueh a bead of pressure as would be obtainable at Bold. Wny the Cor- poration require a min capable of delivering 7,000,000 per day when their whole supply from either Winwick or Bold is only 3,000,000 I do not know. As to my estimates for reservoir and crossings of rail- way and canal, lam prepare I to substantiate them. To recapitutate I have shown- 1. That the supply at Bold is permanent and is over 3,000,000, instead of about 1,000,000 as proposed at
Winwick. 2. That the quality of the Bold water is ideaticil with
the Winwici water. 3. That the 801 l scheme can be carried through for £20,000, or less instead of £lOO,OOO or more, and the water will cow.; the town 21. per 1,000 gallons instead of 4d.

Befere closing my letter I must clear away some by. issues that have been raised. I pointed out that St. Helens and Widees•were taking the same water as tee Bold supply. The Mayor replies that "scarcely any water had been tikea by Sc. Helens from Collins Gr ea Colliery during the Last two years, and that the Corpora- tion of St. Helens heve paid te the company the mini- mum rent of £l,BOO per annum, and have run the bulk of the water down a brook as being unfit to supply to their inhab;tants." The Maycr's iaformant is utterly wrong, and I think ought to apologize to the Collins Green Colliery Cempany. First: There is a clause in the lease that St. Helens can abandon the snpoly if it is unfit for domestic purposes: Second : Sc. Helens does not take all the water pumped at Collins Green (though they use large quantities of it), simply be- cause they have another supply from a higher source, that they can use by gravitation while Collins Green water has to be raised 100. feet to obtain the nelessary pressure at a considerable cost, which lam told amounts to id. per 1,000 gallons. The last point made by the Mayor is that it only costs per 1,070 gallons to pump the Winssick water. I imagine he has taken into account simply the wages and fuel, without including interest on sunk capital, repairs and depreciation. If he will add in these latter items I think he will find that it more nearly approaches my figure of 2.1. per 1.000 gallons than his o l. more, particularly if the? have to lift the water 150 yards instead of 50 yards, as at Winwick. Finally, it is j ist as important to ms as to anyone in Warrington to have a good and cheap water supply. I have such a supply running to waste at Bald, and want to show that it can be utilized at half the cost of the Corporation scheme. If I succeed lam doing a good turn both to the Bold Hall estates and to my native town.—Yours, &c.,
• HENRY FAIRCLOUGH. Chairman of Bold Hall Estitei, Limited.

Sir,—l think it will be generally admitted that the Mayor's mas'cerly reply to Hr. Henry Fair- clou,zh's interesting and able letter proves distinctly that the water schemes advocated by the C3rpara- tion are paramount ti any others that have so far been placed More the public. . .

I would not have -ventured ta have again ad- dressed you in the matter, but that I barn thera is still a slight; opposition to the progress of the Bill. which opposition if persisted in and yet does not clearly demonstrate that the Bill is detrimental to the bast interests of the vrhcile of the community, cannot otherwisa but be characterised, as an act, which though in itself leo% is certainly improper and uncalled for.

In considering the water questim the fact should not be lost sight of, that the water supply is not only one of absolute nec'essitv, but one that is a source of profit to the town. This year I learn that there is expectel to be a profit of £1,833 to the town, and this after providing for the necessary payments in respect of the Capital Fund and interest due thereon. Also that the profit is now increasing at the rata of £5OO a year. The Corporation therefore in seeking powers to extend the Waterworks undertaking are simply asking for powers to extend that which cannot be otherwire described than as a .successful undertaking or buiiness. It should also. be bone in mind that the Corporation will have probably a term of 40 years in which to repay the money which will be required, and which will only be borrowed as it is required. Corporations are allowed to borrow money for terms of from 15 to 75 years, accor ling to the nature of the require- ments, but 40 years I believe will be a fair average to strike in respect of the sums requi-ed by the Bill. The sums required can be borrowed at Irma .E 2 105, £2 153., and .E 2 17s. 61. per cent. on Corporatim Bands, and not as your esteemed correspondent " lona " (whose letters one liivs to peruse) states at from 3to 4 percent. The Corporation of War • rington have and do borrow at the rates I have mentione I. I think all are agreed on the point that shortness of water would not only be a domes. tic calam;ty, but also a suicidal policy so far as manufacturing is concerned. And therefore not to proceed with the schemes would inevitably lead to the town beingicrippled, and men being at times thrown out of employment, besides presenting new works coming into the town. The C3rp)ration have I venture to assert clearly shown:
Ist. That within the next year or two at the presint rate of increase of the town, they will n3t be in a p3sition from the present supply to meet the wants of houieholders and manufacturers..

2nd, That the schemes they advocate by evidence Of expert and graMicil Pan §re the best in ali r - spots for tin town to adopt. 3rd. That the undertaking is being worked at a profit and to the advantage of the whole of the community. lathe face of these facts I ask those who are seeking to binder the Bill from going through t 3 demonstrate clearly to the public, which they have not done so far, that the 03rporation are n'et acting in the best interera of the town—otherwise— withdr w their opp3sitioa and "not put the rate- payers to the turmoil and expense of a •poll, bat al- low the Bill to have a smooth passage through Par- liament.—Yours faithfully, • E. NGLAND.

Haydock, oa Saturday, on the body of John Price Parry, aged 21, of Athol-street, Earlestown, who died at the Cottage Hospital, Hay- dock, on Wednesday last week from injuries re- ceived on September 24th last year, whilst working as a day-wageman in the Princess pit, Haydock, be- longing to ..Vlessrs. R Evans an i Campany. Dr. Hayward, surgeon of the Cottage Hospital said the man was admitted to the hospital in September having had his back injured by a fall of ro3f in the mine. There were symptoms of injury to the spinal chord, but no evidence of fracture or dislocation of tie spine. 'Deceased was partially paralysed in the lower limbs and some of the internal organs pro- bably the result of thelxidneys being injured. He Was no able to get up for two months. On Decent- her 17th by his own desire, deceased left the hospi- tal and went for a few weeks to his home in Wales. He returned.to Earlestown and he became seriously ill. He suffered from influenza which was followed ,by symptoms of inflammation of .the brain. He was removed to the hospital but died ou the We I- nesd ay as stated. Th 3 immed;ate cau-te of death was inflammation of the brain associated with diseases of the kidneys. He had no hesitation in saying that the injury was the primary Cause of death. Hr. H. r 4. Many people in Warrington and diArict will antici- pate With pleasure the return visit of the Rhondda Royal Male Voice Choir which will give a grand evening concert on Tnursday evening next. The choir made such an excellent impression on the occasion of their initial visit to Wairingtm last year that a good house on tee present occasion may be said to be assured. It is admittedly the premier organisation of its kind as its record shows, it being the only male voice society which has won four! National Eist ,Adtodau first priz es,including the 1000 dollars and gold medal at the World's Fair,Chicago. The members have sung before the Qneen at Windsor,and the Duke and Duchess of Westminster at Eaton. The chor, or at least the best part of them, have been twice to Atnerica, and have fre- quently toured in tee Unitel Kingdom. Mr. Tom Stephens, t'le conductor, answering Her Majesty's questions when the concert was over, said that three-fourths of the singers were miners. She told him that the singing was" most magnificent," and , asked for a repetition of " Nien of Ilarlech." When at Eaton Hall, the choir were entertained to supper Iduring which the Duke of Westminster visited them, and expressed on behalf of himself and guests the delight they had experienced by their perform- ances. It may be mentioned that the choir ce.l-:- brates its jubilee this na6nth, when each member is to be presented with a gold medal. No less than 54 first prizes have been won. At the concert on Thursday evening a number of first-class artistes will also appear. They will in- clude • Miss Eleanor Jones, R.C.q. (winner of the open scholarship at the Royal College, and of the Sr. James' and Queen's Hall Concerts London), Mr. 31eurig James, R.A.M. (of the Milan Conservatoire of Music, Italy) Mr. David Davies, and the re- nowned singer of ancient Welsh verses (Pennillion) EO3 Dar. The instrumentalists will be Miss A. Backsheen Wood (solo violinist), Miss Bessie Jones (solo harpist), and Messrs. D. Jones and Percie G. Smith (accompanists). The proceeds are in aid of the Warrington District Nursing Association, an institution which needs no commendation on our part.

(BY A CORRESPONDENT.)

At the Council meeting oa Abnday, there WAS plenty of food for reflection. A week or two ago I alluded to the fact that there had been some grumbling on the part of several tradesmen with respect t 3 their bills for gas consumption during the past quarter, in consequence, as tney stated, of the charge being very much in excess of what it was in the c)rresp3nding period last year. There was plenty of talk Oen of an indignation meeting, but so far nothing has been done in this direction. One or two of the Councillors introduced the sub- ject on Monday, but the Chairman said tee in- creased consumption might be due to the dark nights, or to later hours being kept by persons. Mr. Mclah3n said he was quite satisfied. But I sup- pose there were dark nights last year, and people would no doubt have the same hab t of keeping late hours then, as now. There must be some other explanation of the increase than this.

The sequel to some extent came out in the ap- plication for authority to lay new gas mains for Messrs. AlcCorquodale and C. It would seam that sufficient pressure is not being given to this firm, and in order to meet their requirements, means liave been taken to force the gas through the mains and of course ordinary consumers have had to pay for this extra pressure, without deriving any ma- terial benefit. A motion was brought forward to gb)ut £1,600 in the aying of new gas mains to McCorquodale's works, but it is well known that all the MAilie in the district are too small, and by this time mast be much corroded. They were laid at a time when the towa was in its infancy, so to speak, and although it has grown to respectable proportions,no provision has been made t 3 meet the increased requirements, so far as the mains are con- cerned. The question has evidewly not been lost sight of, and several of the councillors seemed to think that it would be just as well to overhaul all the pip se, and to obtain a loan which would cover the relaying of all the mains as well as providing special pipes for McC)rqualale and Co. Conse- quently an amendment to the m3tion to this effect was pet and carried.

Mr. Brighouse, the County coroner has evidbntly became tired of holding inquecs in public houses, and n) wonder. Same of tile roams are fairly com- fortable and respectable, but in some cases, they are small and stlfff, and I think the last inquest he held in Earlestown, when coroner and jury were al- most overpowered with the heated atmosphere, must have decided him to try for a change. He has applied for the use of a roam at the Town dal], and the Council have very properly acceded to his re- quest. Tee Tawn Hall, when conveniently situated is the proper place for such inquiries.

CHAIRMAN'S ADDRESS.

The Chairman said he felt pretty sure they had all enjoyed the entertainment up to that point and he would endeavour not to mar their pleasure. In the ordinary course of things that would be regarded as their annual ga`hering and that in itself would amply justify them in entertaining feelings of satisfaction and gratification, when they considered the figures read over by the Secre- tary in his repon. It would be rem at once that the year had been a striking one and added a very important page to the annals of the soeiety. They would see that the stacelard of co-operative trading in Earlestown had been raised some distance and planted on a higher eleva- tion until they could confidently say their so- ciety was the greatest trading institution in the district. That gathering was associated with a few important events in the history of the society, the completion and opening of two new branch shops as well as the opening of a butchering department. That department had not been in existence long, hut the sheet experience they had had with it, had every indica- tion of being a success unless they all became vegeta- rians. In connection with the new branch premises, the adoption of toanehee was something entirely new in their society, so that a brief outline of what led up to their achpt'oa might not be out of place. In connection with the branches he might say that the society EOM 3 13 months ago felt in a very similar position to a man whose family had outgrown the accommodation of the modest cottage, and found it necessary to move to a larger house: Tney were in that position some 18 months ago, but they could not enlarge the old shop, and means had to be adopted to meet with the pressure of trade,and they set out to discover whence the main cur- rents of trade came. They found one flowing from Wargrave, one from the Come:ion, and another in Earle- street, where they extended by leasing a shop. In the case of the Common there was no shop to be had, and the one rented in Wargrave-road vas not desirable in more ways than one. They s,lected de- sirable building sites and submitted them to a members' meeting, and they decided to erect two shops thereon. The total amount invested was something like £2.103, that was for everything except the stock. With the completion of these new shops the Socie*oy was now provided with a business capacity equal to £40,000 per annum, and unless the trade of the dis- trict should decline to a great extent,they might reason- ably hope t 3 reach that figure before many years had passed, and when that came to pass the managers of the Society woald come before the members again and ask for a commodious central shop in some part of the town. Some of them might think he was t oci sanguine in these matters, but he was prompted by the increased intelli- gence of the psople. Toeirs was a democratic organis t- ti on of a permanent character which had come to stay. Is was based upon principles that were just and true; its objects were to purify commerce, and there was no power on earth could stay its progress or check its triumphant advance. The programme was then proceeded with,Mr J A Law ringing" Queen of the Earth," and the concert party were applauded for the singing of" A regular royal queen," froin the " The Gondoliers." Mr Winckley afterwards amused the audience with selections on the Gramaphone. After the interval the quartette "Strange Adventure," was given, and Mr Law fellow ed with" I fear no fee." Miss Jennie Johns created amusement with the song and chorus " A bit of string." Mr Shillato gave " A trip to Belle Vise." At this point Mr Parr moved a vote of thanks to the waiters, delegates, chairman aid artistes, and Mr Goff seconded. Mr Mullins alluded to the question of the Society being represented on the District Council and suggested that the chairman, Mr Forrester would make an excellent representative. Mr Gilmour from the audience, rose to speak on the subject, but was not allowed to give expression to his views. Miss Bartle then sang " I could'nt Could I," and Mr Winckley enraptured the audience with his whistling " Biri.VMinaicry." The chorus "ll.M.S.Pinafore " brought the entertainment to a close and after singing " Auld Lang Sy tre " tee audience departed.
SHOP ASSISTANTS' DANCH.

A dance in nnuection with the Warrington Branch of the National Union of Shop Assistants was held at the Druids' Hall, Sankey-street, on Tuesday evening. The company numbered about 50 and Mr. F.A. Fox officiated as M.C. The arrange- ments were well carried out by Messrs. Bradbury and Miller and Mr. J. 11. Toft supplied the refresh- ments. An enjoyable evening was spent, Mr. George Lomas presiding at the piano. LAMPS, Oil Stoves, Coke Stoves, Brass Fenders. Largest seiection.—J. S. GARLAND, Ironmonger, Bridge- street, Warrington.

div.p: FOOTBALL.

Earlestywa did not romp 'nom 3 w:nners on Saturday as they expected. They found 6'kerton were all there, and in fact a mach better team than they hal been led to understand. It certainly was not a team which viiited Haydock, and doubts have been raised whether all the men were eligible to play in a Lancashire junior cap tie. Any way they did play, and Won by 3 goals to 1.

I think the Earlestowa spectators forgot them- seves after the game. The partiality of the referee seamed so apparent that the supporters of the home team treated him to some uncomplimentary observations during the game, and atter it was over they proceeded to stilt stronger measures. The snow which had fallen afforded an excellent weapon of assault, and had it ended there I should have had no fault to find. But they laid violent hands upon him, and rather roughly mauled him, and this is to be regretted. We can all forgive a little excitement, but when it comes to actual assault, there is nothing bat can lemnation for the participation.

Earlestown replay their tie with Bamfurlong in the becond round of the Wigan Cup on Saturday at Bamfurbiag. The team will be the same as that which oppose-1 Skerton on )Saturday, and given a fine day, they should Yang:fish Ba,mfurlong rather easily.

COUNTY OF CHESTER. WILD BIRDS PROTECTION ACTS, 1880, 1894, AND 1896. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the following is a copy of an ORDER which has been made by the Right Honourable Sir Matthew White Ridley, Baronet, M.P., Secretary of State for the Home Department, viz : WILD BIRDS (ENGLAND). The Wild Birds Protection (County of Chester) Order, 1398, 'Dated 15b F bruiry, 1898. In pursuance of the powers conferred upen me by the Wild Birds Protection Acts, 1880 to 1896, and upon application by the County Council of °nester, I hereby snake the following Order,which shall apply tattle whole of the County of Chester :- 1. This Order may be citrd as "The Wild Birds Pro- tection (County of Cnester) Order, 1898." 2. The time during which the killing and taking of wild birds, or any of them, is prohibited by the Wild Birds Protection Act, 1880 (43 and 41 Vic., cap.3s),shall be extended in the County of Chester) so as to be from the Ist day of March to the 12th day of August in each year. 3. The Act of 1880, as extended by Section 2of this Order, shall apply within the whole of the County or Chester to the Kestrel and Heron as if those species were I included in the Schedule of that Act. 4. The taking or killing of the following species of birds, namely :—Kingfisher, Great Crested Grebe,Heron, Goldfinch and Owl, shall be prohibited within the whole of the County of Chester during the whole of that period of the year to which the protection of wild birds under the Act of 1889 (as extended by Section 2 of this Order) does not extend. 5. The taking or destroying of the Eggs of the Owl, Lthee,Biitern, theMingtiehre. the Kestrel, the Heron, the Sheldrake' the Denlin,the Blackheaded G uil,the Common ' Tern, and the Oyster Catcher, shill be prohibited in the whole of the County of Chester. And I make the following further Order, which shall apply within the portion of .the Hundred of Wirral coloured pink on the mapa deposited in the Home Office , and in the office of the County Council, and embrac- , ing the low-lying lands and sandhills situate between 11 the estuaries of the Rivers Dee and Mersey, of which the boundaries shall commence to the south at a point of the main highway of the County of Chester 200 yards to the west of the Dock Cottages near the " Docks " Railway Station of the Wirral IRailway, run along the main highway to Bidston !Village, and then turn in a northerly die ection and run 'to Bidston Railway Station of the earn" Railway, then turn-in a westerly direction and tun along toe Wirral Railway until it reaches the Meols Station of such rail- way, then run along the highway near to the Meols Railway Station in a northerly directon to the Irish Sea then en the north along the margin of high-water mark of the Irish Sea to a point at New Brighton where the Yellow Noses join the said Irish Sea, and then run in a southerly direction to" Warren Drive "or road,and along" Warren Drive "to the mot northerly house and grounds on the west side of such drive, then along the western boundary of the houses and premises situate along the western side of such drive or road to a point 100 yards or so from Grove-road then turning in a westerly direction along the northern boundaries of the houses and premises in Grove-road, Wallasey, until it leachea the Wirral Railway, then turning in a southerly direcVon along the Wirral Railway until it reaches the Wallasey Marsh, then along the edge of the marsh in a southerly direction until it reaches the Poulton Half- penny Bridge, then turning in a westerly direction on the edge of the said marsh, until it reaehes along the edge of tlee marsh the main highway leading from Poul- ton to Meols, such parts within the aforesaid boundaries as are market garden lands and are not coloured in the said maps are excepted from the operation of this Order. 6, The Act of 1880. as extended by Section 2of this Order, shall apply within the above-named area to the following species of birds -- Red-backed Shrike, Whinchat, Spotted Flycatcher, Sedge Warbler, Blackcap Warbler, Grasihopper Warbler Wood Warbler, Garden Warbler, Mistle Thrush,Common Bunting, Reed Bunting, Goldfinch, Wheatear, Chiffchaff, Golden-crested Wren, Yellow Wagtail, Pied Wagtail, Water Wagtail. Skylark, and Titlark, as if they were in- cluded in the Schedule to the Act of 1880. 7. The taking or destroying of the Eggs of all Wild Birds shall be prohibited within the above-named area for a period of five years from the date of this Order. 8. The taking or killing of ALL WILD BIRDS shall be prolaib:ted within the above-named area during the whole of that period of the year to which the protection of wild birds under the Act of 1580 as extended by Sec- tion 2 of this Order does not extend. 9. The taking or killing of the Gull and the Tern is prohibited within the Administrative County of Chester during the whole of that period of the year to which the protection of wild birds under the Wild Birds Protection Act, 1880 (as extended by Stction 2 of this Order) does I act extend. 10. I hereby exempt from the operatio.e of paragraph , number 901 this Order so much of the County of Chester I as does NOT lie within the Parishes of PUDDINGTON WALL 9,SEY BURTON LOWER BEBINGTON NESS BROMBOROUGH NESTON-CUM-PARKGATE Bosnia" BOOTON INCE INETHERPOOL GREAT STANNEY 1 WHITBY FRODSHAM LORDSHIP STANLOW I,VESTON GIYTON IINCORN lIESWALLeCUM- HALTON OLDFIELD NORTON THURSTASTON MOORE CALDY ACTON GRANGE HOYLAKE-CUM-WFST WALTON INFERIOR KIRBY Including therein so much of the estuaries of the Rivers Dee and Mersey as lies witbiti the Administrative County of Chester. 11. On Friday evening last week in the Museum Lec- ture Room, Mr. W. Holbrook read a paper on " Spiders and their habits," embodying many of the observations made during an evidently patient and careful, as well as enthusiastic study of spiders curing the past two summers. He made use of a series of diagrams tl illustrate certain aspects of the subject, showed a number of specimens preserved in spirit, an I has had the satisfaction of recordiug three species, new to the district, viz, Lycasa pieta, Slicaria pulicara, and Harpactes hombergii. An in- teresting discussion followed. Mr. W. Cartwright, of Moore, als) read a paper entitled" Apia melli- flea:4 He explained a number of experiments and observations wi-ich he had made, and succeeded in giving the members of the club a very vivid pioture of the lite and economy of these insects. There was a consensus of opinion that both papers (which were maiden efforts) were worthy of the best tradi- lions of thc club.

WARRINGT ON CYCLING CLUB. 41:30 Per Centi, ANNUAL MEETING. OF There was a very encouraging attendance at the an- nual general meeting of this club, held at the headquir- , HUMAN AILMENTS ters, Patton Arms Rotel, Warrington, on Thursday last ' RESULT FROM A week. Mr C Wood occupied the chair, and he was ac- companied at the head of the table by Mr E Pickavance, TORPID LIVER jun., and Mr A Booth ,the hon. secretaries of the club. SECRETARIES' REPORT. Mr PICRAVANCE said in presenting the 13th annual re- OR port of the Warrington Cycling Club they could safely WEAK KIDNEYS. claim to have had a most successful season. The weather though rather wet in the early poet of the eear.inaproved as the season advanced and most of their functions were carried out under the most favourable circumstances. The WARNER'S " SAFE " CURE opening run was again to Cronton and the wisdom of that cho'ce was proved by the fact that 50 members turned out and had a good time. The Easter toar was to Bala and owing to the fine day on Geod Friday 18 members turned up at that pretty We'sh village. A good time was spent, but for cycling purposes there was 'rather a superfluity of moisture to make the out a p'!r- feet success. (Laughter) May 3rd was the opening Tuesday night run and 40 members turned up at Sankey Chapel House, and had a goad smoker. On IJune the 28th the over popular bowling main was started, an 4 after heats had been played at Sankey Chapel House, Newton Whiston and Stre...tton the first prize was wen by J Irineelow. H Whittle on- timing the second, and J T Farrinston third, and F A [Jones fourth. On Seurday, July 9th, they were again the guests of their valued vice-president, Mr. Naylor a t IBeeston Tower. The inter-club run with the Msechoster Wheelers took place and a most enjoyable afternoon was spent at Davenham. On September 12;11 the annual fish- ing match was held at Lymin on the Warrington Anglers' Association's preserve, which was most gener- ously lent for the occasion. After an exciting contest the first prizes was won by W S Barker, and the second by .1 Podmore. The raging men of the club owing to various indispositions and unavoidable circumstaaces had not been very successful and they regretted that not a single N.C.U., medal had come to the club this season. The touring members hal been again busy. and Ncrth Wales. the Lake district and the Norfolk Broads had been visited. The attendance at club runs ea I been again most satisfactory the average attendance t eing 25. The attendance medals for Satur- day and Tuesday runs combined, had been won by W Litton. and John Ray, whilst the Tuesday night medal was won by James Ray. The medals were presented to the club by the president, Councillor W. Pierpoint. The winter programme had been varied and successful. Reference was made to the billierd handicaps, hot pot supp.rs and smokers, and the annual dance. The treasurer's balance sheet showed the club was on a sounder financial basis than last year. The committee meetings had been well attended and it had been a pleasure to work with such an unanimous and enthusiastic committee. The thanks of the club were also due to the local and cycling papers for their excel- lent reports. Mr. Lerroer oroposed the adoption of the report. Mr. Warhurst seconded, and the report was adopted. THE BALANCE SHEET. 1 In the absences of Mr Mounfield, (the hon. treasurer), Mr Beath read the financial statement. The year com- menced with a balance in hand of £5 is 2d, and the- total receipts including £2O 9s. Od. for members sub serietions, amonnted to £55 2s. 9d. The expenses were £4B 81 si, leaviog a balance to be carried forward of £6 14s 4d.—The report was adopted. VOTES OF THASKS. A vote of thanks was accorded the secretaries—Messrs Piceavanee and Booth ; also to the treasurer, Mr Moun- field ; the captain ; vice-captains ; the auditors ; the press, and the committee. ELECTION OF PRESIDENT. Mr PICEAVANCE proposed the re-election of Councillor Pierpeint. He thought that gentleman made a very s it stile president. (Rear, hear.) Be had presided at several of their functions and had given them three valuable medals. He had also promised prizes for the billiard handicap.—Mr Hulse secoeded the proposition and it was unanimously agreed to. THE VICE-PRESIDENTS. The retiring vice-presidents were re-elected with one or two exception!. The name of Captain Waring was added to the Het, and Mr. J.F. Kiernan' name was sub- stituted for that of his father, eceased. THE SECRETARIES AND OTHER OFFICERS. Mr. LITTON proposed the re-elgction of Mr. Picks- vance and Mr. Booth as boa. secretaries. Mr. Picks.- Vance was an easy first for the position of vice-president on the N.C.U. and they ought to be very proud of him, (Hear, hear.) Mr. Hulse s.conded, aed the resoltrion was enthusiastically carried, wad the secretaries re- turned thanks.—The auditors—M,sesre. F. Barber and B &try were also re-elEc:ed.—Tee Cheirm in pointed out that they had had an increase of 21. members during the past ear. (Hear, hear.) THE CAPTAIN AND SUB-CAPTAIN. Balletieg took place for these p isitions. The SCIII- tineers reported that Mr George Smith had received the highest number of votes tor the captaiecy, and Mr Clare for the sub-captaincy. COMMITTEE. The following were appointed on the committee : Messrs W Brown, C H Wood, W H Bellian, W Litton, J Podmore, T J Hulse, and Davenport. Tees was all the business.

THE ST. HELENS MURDER. QUESTION IN PARLIAMENr. In the House of Commons yesterday afternoon, Mr. Davitt asked the Home Secretary with reference to the case of a child, six years old, the daughter of a collier named Flaherty, who was outraged and then murdered, near Sc. Helens in December last, what steps were taken by the loam pZce to discov!r the auth3r of the crime ; whether the Home Office sapplemented these steps, and, if so, in what manner; and whether any Clue of any kind has been obtained up to the present, to lead a hope that the murderer may be discovered? The Home Secretary said —I have not had any infor• illation whatever on the subject of the ques:ion, but I am making inquiries, and if the hon. gentleman will put his question down at a later date, I may be able to answer it.
